utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I fear there was probably a slip or breakdown in communication last week about the witness for today. It was our understanding that following the two previous occasions when the witness, Professor Kristan, had been available for court but hadn't been capable of being called, it was our understanding that following that he was a fixed witness for today. The fixture being in large part required by the limitations on the amount of time there would be available for using Slovenian interpreters. That limitation we understand to be in effect today and that the interpreters are available in the Slovenian language only for today and we had understood that to be known to all parties, and therefore, we had understood it to be understood that it would be Professor Kristan being interposed this morning, which is our intention. I'm very sorry this wasn't clarified with the Court in open court last week, but I hope that the Chamber is content for Professor Kristan to be called in order that the accused may have enough time to cross-examine him with the Slovenian interpreters present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, none of that was indicated to the Court, and it wasn't until Friday afternoon that we received a message to the effect that that was so and that the Slovenian interpreters were only here for a day. These matters really must be indicated in good time to the Trial Chamber and to the accused in order that the trial can run properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I entirely agree, and the fact that one party thought the other had made the communication and the other party thought the first party had is no excuse. We should have made it clear to you. Nevertheless, the accused has been on notice that this is our intention, and although the witness is himself flexible, for reasons of the limitations placed on us by availability of Slovenian interpreters, I'd ask that we take him today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we will allow that, but of course there must be time, if there's only one day available, for adequate cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I -- as the Court knows, Professor Kristan is not allowed to give evidence in relation to matters about Kosovo's autonomy and its revocation and the rights to self-determination. What we've done in those circumstances and bearing in mind that although he's not at our hand subject to questioning on those topics, the accused has already indicated he may ask more broadly about various topics. What we've done is prepare an exhibit bundle which I think has 20 -- currently has 20 -- 30 tabs in it. It contains a range of constitutional documents, and with your leave may we review at the end of all the evidence which one should stand and which one should be withdrawn? You'll see that this does still contain some of the basic Kosovo documents in case they turn up. Alternatively, the Chamber may want them produced in any event without any comment on them by the witness so that those documents can be referred to by any later constitutional expert we're able to call. The Chamber also has a short summary and associated with the summary a set of charts. May the charts in due course become an exhibit perhaps as part of or as an exhibit in sequence with the report itself, and I will be getting the expert to summarise the effect of his admissible report by reference to those charts, and may he come in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. I do not appear to have the summary. Where should it be?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. Coming straight away.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have the summary either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you have a copy for the interpreters of the summary?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Coming their way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Dr. Kristan, if you would take the declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is your full name Ivan Kristan?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You are Slovenian by birth. You are a retired professor of constitutional law from the University of Ljubljana where indeed you were dean of the faculty of law between 1981 and 1985, also having served as Justice of the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia in Belgrade from 1987 to 1991 and having been president of the Slovenian Second Chamber of the National Council of the Republic of Slovenia between 1992 and 1997?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes. The Constitutional Court, I was not its president. I was the deputy president, but I was the president of the State Council of the Republic of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you prepare at the request and instruction of the Office of the Prosecutor a report which has been filed publicly on the constitutional and legal issues -- or some of the constitutional and legal issues arising in this case?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes. At the request of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Professor Kristan, we are very pressed for time. And wherever a question is susceptible to the answer yes or no, it would help us, although I know it's an inconvenience, if you could just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As you appreciate, it's not necessary for us to go through your expert report in detail or indeed at all because the accused has had an opportunity to read it and of course to be advised of it. Nevertheless, in order to give a broad understanding for those viewing the trial of what your evidence amounts to, have there been prepared some charts in respect of which you're able to make comments, the charts representing in graphic form the conclusions your report makes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the first of those charts be placed on the overhead projector, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have my own version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Here comes another one, the latest version incorporating the amendments that you considered yesterday afternoon, and does the first chart deal with the SFRY 1974 constitution in the absolute broadest of outlines, showing -- and we've got it up on the screen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think the ELMO is working.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While that technical problem is being addressed -- while that technical problem is being addressed and to avoid wasting time, since the witness and the Chamber has the first chart, this chart shows on the left-hand side, Professor Kristan, the six republics and the two semi-autonomous regions of Vojvodina and Kosovo, part of Serbia but nevertheless with very substantial rights. It then shows on the right-hand side the SFRY Presidency with its eight members coming one from each republic, one from each autonomous province of whom one member was elected president for one year. Now, drawn between those two, as people will see when the ELMO is functioning publicly, is a circle or oval with the Presidents of the Republics and the Autonomous Provinces identified within that circle, and you've then drawn or we've drawn, to represent your conclusions, a solid line going to the left to the republic themselves but a dotted line going towards the Presidency. Was there any formal relationship between the presidents of the republics or the presidents of the autonomous provinces and the members of the SFRY Presidency coming from the same republic or autonomous province?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: The -- as far as a formal relationship of superiority or subordination didn't exist. Members of the Presidency of SFRY from the republics or provinces had a relationship with their respective Assemblies that elected them, and they were accountable to them and not to the president or Presidencies of the republics or provinces. The president of Republic of Serbia, for example, could replace its member of the SFRY Presidency in case he was -- this person was not in a position to occupy his post.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One more question only on this chart. In order to give us an idea of the degree, or the way in which, rather, the autonomous provinces approached the status of republics, was there something called a principle of parity? If so, please explain.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: This was the only case in the constitutional system of Yugoslavia where the autonomous provinces were on equal footing with the republic. The republics were considered states while the autonomous provinces were not. However, the level of parity of the autonomous provinces with the republics was rather high. And as far as the membership in the SFRY Presidency, the autonomous provinces were in parity, in a position of parity with the republics. But in the Federal Assembly, in the two Chambers, the parity did not exist. In the Federal Chamber, the first chamber, the republics were represented with 30 members, and from the autonomous provinces 20. And the second chamber, 12 members from each of the republics and eight members from the autonomous provinces. So they had fewer -- fewer representatives. But they were -- they -- in 1946, for example, there was a difference in the status of the two provinces; Vojvodina had a higher status and Kosovo a lower one constitutionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's turn to chart number 2. As we do that, may the report itself be given an exhibit number, and may the charts, which I think should be exhibited, become either a part of that or a following exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which is going to be convenient? At the moment, we have the main exhibits which can be given one number. I should think it better if the charts get another number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The report will be P524. The chart will be P525, and the rest 526.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And, Your Honour, it may be that in my brief examination of the witness in chief I won't take time to go to any of the exhibits. In due course, it may be a proper approach to decide which have been produced to see which he's asked about in any cross-examination and which are identified in his report, because they plainly should be themselves exhibited. We'll tidy that up at the end of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Chart 2, and if it's not operating on the -- it's unfortunate -- ah, there it is. Chart 2 deals with the position under the 1974 constitution so far as Defence is concerned, reproduces the passage in the first chart identifying the SFRY itself and the Presidency. We note that under the Presidency, there's the Supreme Command constituted by the president of the -- or allowing the president of the Presidency to be a supreme commander. We then see that you've drawn -- or we've drawn, to reflect your report, a line going down to the Federal Secretary for People's Defence, with whom the Chamber is already familiar. Coming down from that box to the Chief of the General Staff of the SFRY armed forces - and you've then put down JNA and Territorial Defence - we see a solid line going from the right of the Federal Secretariat for People's Defence down the right towards Military Districts, and underneath Military Districts we see solid lines leading to ovals containing the initials JNA and also Territorial Defence. Sticking with the solid lines, we see on the top left lines coming from the republics and autonomous provinces down towards the Territorial Defence with a solid line marked 1988 coming down towards and linking to both the Chief of General Staff and the Military Districts. Separately from those lines we see a dotted line marked pre-1988 going from the Territorial Defence to the Presidency, and a different format of dotted line going from the Territorial Defence to the Presidents of the Republics and Autonomous Provinces. Now, we have to be very brief, and that's why we hope these charts will help us, Professor. The -- just one minute. The lines on the right-hand side, do they describe really rather conventionally the command of the Supreme Command via the secretary, federal secretary, and via the Chief of the General Staff for both military districts and the JNA and the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Here I would like to draw the attention to the difference which was introduced in 1998, namely the difference between the status between the JNA and the TO. The JNA was a unified armed force with the General Staff, while Territorial Defence was directly linked to the Presidency. The Territorial Defence consisted of eight parts. Each of the republics and the autonomous provinces had their TOs, and they were linked directly to the Presidency. After that, a change took place when the Chief of General Staff was introduced and the army and the Presidency and the Territorial Defence came under the General Staff. After that, other changes were introduced with the introduction of four strategic military districts and the subordination of the army and the Territorial Defence was in this sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just to underline the point you've made, the republics had -- and the autonomous provinces had Territorial Defence, but they had no component part of the army. That was dealt with on a federal basis; correct?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes. Territorial Defence was organised in the republics and the provinces. That was the sense of it in order to ensure all people's resistance on the territory. And the Territorial Defence was linked to the bodies and institutions of the republics and provinces. The Territorial Defence had a commander, commander who was accountable to the president of the republic or the Presidency in order to -- concerning matters of organisation of defence. So we had the Presidency, the -- then the Chief of General Staff. That was the sequence of subordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two more short questions, both on dotted lines shown on this chart. The dotted line on the right-hand side of the chart between the Chief of the General Staff and the Military Districts is said to be one of communication. So how were the military districts commanded? We can see that they were commanded by the Federal Secretary for People's Defence because there's a solid line there, and we can see other solid lines coming down from the left-hand side. What's the significance of that little dotted line, please?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: It would be difficult to describe this distinction. You have to take into account the chain of command. At the head of it was the SFRY Presidency, which could move and entrust certain competencies to the Federal Secretary of People's Defence. From there to the CGS and then down to the Military Districts. How -- as far as the differences in communication goes, I couldn't elucidate on that. I must say that I do not know exactly how this occurred. But this is the chain of command from the Presidency downwards to the Military Districts which cover the units of the JNA and of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, on the middle and towards the top left of the chart, we see a dotted line linking the Presidents of the Republics at an angle to the Territorial Defence of the Republics and Autonomous Provinces. Can you explain that? What it says on the legend is that personnel, organisation, and equipment of the Territorial Defence and how in October 1987 the Chief of the General Staff became the Chief of the General Staff of the armed forces. Can you explain that line, please, for us.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Concerning this dotted line from the SFRY Presidency to the Territorial Defence, as I have mentioned earlier, was that the TO was organised within the republics and provinces, and it is here that the level of -- high level of competencies was, and responsibilities towards the presidents of the respective republics, and the Territorial Defence commander wasn't only responsible to the SFRY -- president of the Presidency or the Federal Secretary but to the presidents of the republics and of the autonomous provinces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we look now at chart number 3, it seeks to summarise under the same 1974 constitution the position in relation to the police. The top part of the chart now already familiar. And indeed, on the right-hand side we see the same reflection of SSNO, CGS, Military Districts. Underneath Military Districts we've now added to the JNA and the Territorial Defence the police for the republics and autonomous provinces, and towards the left we've got an oval with the police connected by solid lines coming from the republics and autonomous provinces and coming down to join solid lines from the CGS and the Military Districts. What was the position of the police? How did it change in one of the three states with which the Chamber is already familiar?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: I've understood this question as a question of subordination of the Minister of Interior to the Minister of the Republic, and here I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. indicated that the police was not under the subordination of the president but that it was a part of the government and it functioned on the basis of the law of the government, and the president of the republic had a position vis-a-vis the government. He also appointed the possible -- president of the government gave him the mandate. So as far as the police was concerned in case of war, imminent threat of war, the police was subordinated to the military and to the Supreme Commander, the SFRY Presidency, and only in this sense it would make sense to include the police here in case of -- and make it subordinated in case of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But in the absence of one of those three states, by whom were the police commanded?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: It was commanded by the JNA commander. The police was -- it had also a question of accountability. It was -- but otherwise, it's a part of the Ministry of Interior. It has the tasks of assuring peace and order, public order, and in a normal situation, it doesn't have a defence function.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we turn from this chart we see no reference on it to either volunteers or paramilitary groups. Did they have any identified legal status within the constitution or not? Indeed, were they legal or were they outlawed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: The paramilitary units were not legal. Volunteers were legal, but they had to organise on the basis of a provision issued on the basis of the law on defence and all people's protection that in case of imminent threat of war or war, in order to replenish the ranks of the military. In these cases, the volunteers received a status of soldier, and on the basis of this provision, decree of the Presidency ensured that the status of volunteers was regulated and in order to avoid any possibilities of paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we turn now, please, to chart 4 which summarises or seeks to summarise changes between 1988 and 1992 that may be material to assist the Chamber here. We see in the box that you list some changes and the numbers of your list or our list reflecting your report are then repeated at various places on the chart so that the first change, the 1988 to 1999 so-called Anti-Bureaucratic Revolutions in Montenegro and Vojvodina find themselves reflected in the figure 1 on the chart. The result of that was what, please, as you understood it, the result of those Anti-Bureaucratic Revolutions?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: The meaning of those Anti-Bureaucratic Revolution rallies was the destabilisation in the province, province of Vojvodina where it began. And the -- it -- the existing ordinance were replaced both in Vojvodina and Montenegro. Such a meeting of truth was also planned for the 1st of December of 1989 in Slovenia. However, Slovenia opposed it, and the Ministry of Interior prohibited it. This attempt of destabilisation, an individual stopped at that point when this meeting of truth didn't take place in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Number 2 mentions Kosovo and Vojvodina. As you know, your opinions on these matters are not a topic upon which the Chamber seeks your assistance, but as a matter of fact. Just for a chronological point of view between 1989 to 1991, may it be said that there was a revocation, as a matter of fact, of the autonomy of Kosovo and Vojvodina and you've therefore reflected that by the figure 2 in the chart. Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: This was a continuity of these events of the Anti-Bureaucratic Revolution. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I just really want -- because of the limitations placed on your report by the Trial Chamber, we just need it as a fact that the revocation occurred if that be correct.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes. In 1989, this procedure began with the amendment, then with certain laws concerning Kosovo, and then the revocation was completed with the Serbian constitution of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then as a matter of fact, following that revocation --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really believe that these are key issues linked to the autonomy -- to autonomy in general, and the expert cannot go beyond the chapters allowed by you. You allowed that we hear his expert opinion in connection with all the points mentioned after page 33. However, all that was said just now relates to matters having to do with the revocation of the autonomy and the right to self-determination, and I think you have ruled about that already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness is limited merely to dealing with the fact and no more than that. So we will not allow him to go any further. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. From the summary, the third bullet point -- and again I simply want this as a fact, I don't want any expression of opinion, as I've made clear. Following these changes, and thus in July 1990, was Kosovo participating separately in the decision-making of the Federation? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Kosovo, according to the constitution of Yugoslavia, participated in the decision-making of the Federation. It was in the structure of the federal organs, and it was represented there, as we have already said, according to the principle of parity in the Presidencies while in other organs the representation was lower. But in all organs, the autonomous provinces, including Kosovo, were included in decision-making at the federal level.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: After the revocation of autonomy, did that participation cease? Please just yes or no. Did the participation cease following revocation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: It did -- it did cease. It did cease in its basic elements. The provinces could not participate in the decision-making on some issues. First, Kosovo where the Presidency was abolished and then the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. If we then turn to the next item on your list of changes, our list of changes reflecting the contents of your report: On the 15th of March of 1991, did the SFRY Presidency reject proposals to introduce a state of emergency?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've heard evidence about this. Mr. Mesic gave evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Indeed he did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not getting any interpretation, but in fact, we've heard evidence about this, so we needn't go over it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. In which case can we go on in the summary to what the witness refers to in his report on page 11 as happening on the 17th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As a matter of historical fact, what did the accused make clear in the statement on the 17th of March, Professor Kristan?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This witness is supposed to be an expert, giving us evidence about the constitution, which he's done so far. You're now, Mr. Nice, moving into different ground, in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, let me come back to that if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And matters, if I may add, of which we've heard evidence. We don't need to go over it again and we certainly don't need, with respect to the witness, his interpretation. He can deal with the matters which he has dealt with heretofore, which are the constitutional matters. Evidence about them is appropriate, but not about the facts which are, after all, the things we're going to have to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Then I'll come beyond those items in the sequence to the 1st of October's decision on the imminent threat of war and the amendments to the Presidency's rules of procedure that followed that on the 3rd of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In your judgement, what was the effect of the decision on the 1st of October?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Well, this was the proclamation of the imminent threat of war by the Presidency. However, I was looking for grounds for this proclamation, and this is also summarised in the documentation after the Tanjug agency in the draft of the minutes. I did not find any resolution or conclusion on that the Presidency would adopt such a conclusion on the threat of an imminent war in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 3rd of October, there was a change in the decision-making rules and change in the quorum, I think. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: This is linked. If there is a suspicion about the decision on the proclamation of the imminent threat of war was on the 1st of October, well, then this suspicion is prolonged to the 3rd of October, and in addition, when the Presidency starts working under the conditions of imminent threat of war, well, there is an additional problem, because at this particular session, the Presidency did not have the required quorum for decision-making, neither the majority for adopt such a resolution. This means that this is an illegal act.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You also deal - and this is not on the chart - or are able to deal with the decision under rules of procedure for the SFRY to sit continuously in Belgrade, this decision following the declaration of imminent threat of war. What do you say about the decision to sit permanently in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was indeed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please look at paragraph 197 of the report. The expert said what he can say as an expert. He stated very clearly this means that four members of the Presidency of the SFRY could not function on behalf of the Presidency of the SFRY. I think that this has been explicitly stated and there's no need for him to go into the decisions that were taken. He stated that very clearly, and I think there's nothing more to add to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let counsel take whatever course he thinks appropriate. We'll bear in mind the points you made and indeed you can cross-examine the witness about them. Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What do you say of the decision to sit permanently in Belgrade, which is covered by exhibits - we don't need to turn to them necessarily - but what do you say about their effect and legality?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Well, this is related to the same session, and this decision, of course, concerning a transfer to a state of emergency was, of course, illegal, and it was also illegal that the Presidency may have taken decisions by a majority vote of its members, as would usually be the case for a Presidency, because this decision had not been taken, in fact, in a valid way. And this obviously now would represent an additional difficulty for those members of the Presidency that were not physically present in Belgrade, for instance, for Mesic in Zagreb, Trnosek in Ljubljana, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last entry on this chart number 4, numbered 5 on the left-hand side, relates to the SFRY presidential order of the 10th of December whereby engagement of volunteers in the SFRY armed forces during the imminent threat of war was dealt with, and we can see that reflected in a new oval box at the bottom right-hand corner of the chart. Explain that, please, to us.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: I have already mentioned it in passing. This was paragraph 251 from my report, and that was the formal system as laid down in greater detail regulating the status of volunteers whereby they were part of the armed forces, had to abide by military discipline and eliminating thereby also paramilitary units. And all these units within ten days had to coordinate their status with this particular decision or order on volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We move then to chart number 5, which in summary form deals with some changes in Serbia at the time of or following the 1990 constitution. You might like to speak generally to the chart and then I'll pick up whatever you haven't dealt with. Can you explain, using this chart and in short form, what changes were effected particularly in the power of the president by the 1990 constitution?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: With your permission, I would like to point out that the whole procedure of change in Serbia had begun already with the adoption of amendments in 1989, the 23rd of March, 1989, especially because these also regulated relations with autonomous provinces. Furthermore, also essential changes with the change in the Serbian constitution on the 28th of September 1990, and this was of course quite essential in terms of revocation of autonomy. As far as the executive is concerned and the president of the republic, well, in fact, that meant strengthening the status of the president and his powers in relation to the former Presidency and the status of the president now becomes very strong by this constitution. Additionally, also this position of the president was furthermore determined by the law on defence with the express functions that the president had as head of the executive power in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. We see that you -- or we've drawn to reflect the position solid lines between the oval in which the words "President of Serbia" are written, and Serbia on the left, and the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia on the right. What was his relationship with the Assembly, for example?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Well, here the president on the one hand had a conventional relation and his function being, for instance, proposing the mandatory and so forth, the officials, top officials. On the other hand, the president of the republic also enjoyed a sort of priority because he was directly elected while there was this possibility for recall as well. However, a very high majority would have been required in this case, and also with the voting majority of the electorate. In relation to the Assembly, actually the president was autonomous, was independent. On the other hand, the strong position of the president was also reflected in his position at the Supreme Command as Supreme Commander and also his right of taking decisions on the basis of the constitution as regards, for instance, the state of emergency or extraordinary circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His direct election, did that make him usual or unique within the organs of the republics of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Well, he was not the only official directly elected. However, he had the strongest position as per constitution. And he was directly elected, for instance, and he was given a higher authority in the public. However, he was not as strong or as independent as the president of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you leave 5, Mr. Nice, perhaps you could assist us with the circle of Armed Forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was going to turn to that, and in particular it was a question mark between that and Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The position of the president in relation to the armed forces is shown on our map by a solid line, initially grey but nevertheless solid going to the Armed Forces. And there's a question mark not very clearly shown, but beneath that there is a double-ended arrow going to Territorial Defence and Volunteers. Can you explain why we've drawn it in that way as reflected in your report.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Well, this was a change that occurred in Serbia then because this was not the case in other republics, namely by amending the constitution in 1990, Serbia actually revoked the institute of Territorial Defence in Serbia. We no longer find it in the 1990 constitution. Whereas in the law on defence of 1991, the Territorial Defence was introduced, and it was laid down in express terms on the basis of a definition well known in Yugoslavia then. And the Serbian constitution actually referred to the armed forces of Serbia, only the armed forces. And the president of the republic was its Commander-in-Chief. And this question mark implies that actually it is not clear what the armed forces of Serbia are, how they are defined, because a law on defence -- on armed forces had been announced, however, to my knowledge it Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. had not been passed. Therefore, it is not quite clear what the armed forces of Serbia refer to. However, the law on defence speaks of a Territorial Defence, and we can assume that the Territorial Defence units were in fact the armed forces of Serbia to represent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The lines linking the President of Serbia to the police are probably more --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The accused wants to raise something, I believe, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: A minute? Yes. We'll rise for a minute, two minutes. --- Break taken at 10.01 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the chart, Professor Kristan, the dotted lines linking the President of Serbia to the police, either separately or via the government of the Republic of Serbia, speak for themselves when we see the legend says that this relates only to war or the imminent threat of war. And I have one other question to you ask about volunteers. Was there a decree on the registration of volunteers on the 13th of August, 1991 and if so, what did it affect or achieve?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: As far as volunteers are concerned, I've already explained why they were instituted, and there was this decree of December as well as the decree in Serbia to regulate the status of volunteers. And this was, as far as the dotted line is concerned, between the President of Serbia and police. Well, there again, this -- the meaning is that the President of Serbia, in exceptional circumstances, this is explained in 276 of paragraph -- of the report, he could, for instance, recruit police as well as certain other elements as far as the composition of the police force is concerned. So much about this relationship. Otherwise, police is part and parcel of the Ministry of the Interior and as such was part of the government -- the governmental system and its policy, and there was no direct subordination -- subordination to the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, volunteers, the legend says, can be used to reinforce the Territorial Defence of Serbia during one of the three states. Do we have to distinguish volunteers from paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Well, indeed the meaning of this formal determination of the status on the basis of the two decrees indeed was there to separate them from the paramilitary units to know what units are illegal and what are the units active within the armed forces and have to abide by the necessary discipline, including also the law -- the legislation on war. And this relates both to the military units or the police force that would be also included in or involved, for instance, in any kind of violation of the military -- of the war law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So volunteers could become lawful contributors to the armed forces. Paramilitaries, were they ever in a position to become lawful contributors to the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Paramilitary units could not make legal their status unless within the framework of this decision on the decree on regulating the status of volunteers. If, for instance, they adapted to the decree on registration of volunteers, in that case they would become volunteers and would also have to abide by the military order and would be subordinated to the military command and in the final analysis or so to the Supreme Command of the armed forces. That was the meaning of this. Paramilitary units were illegal, and it would have only been possible to register them within the framework of this decree and also with a time limit set, and that was a ten-day time limit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did that happen as a fact that paramilitary units legalised themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I do not have this information. I have not been following what was happening, but I presume this was the case. Those units which had not registered themselves were considered as illegal units, and they did or they should have prosecuted such units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want to move swiftly to the conclusion of your examination-in-chief because of the passage of time, so can we go to chart number 6. Tab 6 shows the FRY April 1992 Constitution in the boldest of outlines, this new state being adopted on the 27th of April, 1992, constituted by Serbia and Montenegro, as we already know. What do you say as to the validity of the adoption of this constitution and body?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Well, I would say here it is possible to discuss this issue, to comment this issue from the constitutional and legal point of view. I'm referring to the procedure of the adoption of the constitution of Yugoslavia on the 27th of April, 1992. What is it about? The constitution was passed and proclaimed by the Federal Chamber of the Assembly of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, i.e., of another, of a different state, not of the same state of which the constitution was being passed at the time. As a constitutional lawyer, I conclude that the Federal Chamber of the Assembly of SFRY was not competent, did not have the required powers to pass this constitution and to proclaim it. Neither was it operational, because according to the constitution of Yugoslavia, for the work of the federal Assembly a quorum was required, i.e., the majority of all the MPs of the Federal Chamber. And as we know, the Federal Chamber consisted of 30 MPs of each republic and 20 MPs from each autonomous province, and half of these MPs represented the quorum for the work of the Federal Chamber. But as it is known, only two republics participated in the proclamation, and only the deputies, the MPs of two republics, of these two republics. According to the data I found in the media, around 70 -- a bit more than 70 MPs were present at that session, and from this point of view, the Federal Chamber was not competent and not operational in order to perform this act.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The chart shows the composition of the Supreme Defence Council, with which the Chamber is familiar, composed at one stage of the three presidents, the two of the republics and the one of FRY itself, they operating through the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ to the army, air force, and navy. The voting system of the Supreme Defence Council is something with which we are also familiar, it changing from majority to consensus. Do you have any comments on the change in the voting system of the council or not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Well, this Defence Council was a very special body. It consisted of three members, i.e., the president of FRY - of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia - and of the presidents of the two federal unit -- units. Well, this composition was complicated, because formally all the three members were equal. However, the president, on the basis of his position, had a certain advantage in relation to the remaining two. The president was the one to put forward the initiatives for the work, he was the one to take care for the implementation of the decisions, and he had a much stronger position in the joint bodies as well. In particular, as the person who also was the commander of the federal -- of the federal armed forces. And he was also the president of the Supreme Defence Council. Vis-a-vis the Federal Assembly of Yugoslavia, his position was similar to the position of a head of state. He had the powers of proposals and of initiative. The difference between the two -- well, in this case this president is not directly elected but is elected by the federal -- Federal Assembly. The term of office is four years. Only one election is possible. While in the case of the president of Serbia, as we could see before, the president of Serbia was elected directly, it was possible to revoke the president of Serbia, however, the conditions to do this were very demanding. And the president of Serbia also had the power of dissolving the Assembly of the republic. This, however, was not so at the case of the federal constitution. If --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, go on.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes. If, for example, the Assembly for a longer period of time would not discharge its -- its duties, the government could resolve the Assembly of Yugoslavia. The Assembly of Yugoslavia was composed on the parity principle basis, 20 MPs from each unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want quite literally one-line answers to the following questions so that we can know what your position is, you being in a position to answer questions to the accused on these topics if he raises them. They're under Miscellaneous in the summary. In your opinion - just yes or no - was SFRY and its armed forces bound to humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By what -- similarly brief answer, please, or as brief as can possibly be made: By what legal means could the accused have retained Yugoslavia as a united state?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Here I see as a legal means, I see no other than the parliamentary democratic means. An agreement would have to be achieved between the members of the Federation, and then along the legal route undertake the change of the constitution. Regrettably, this did not take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Similar question: In your judgement as a constitutional lawyer, was there a way in which the Serbs in Croatia could have declared independence and achieved autonomy legally?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: I believe not. Here I must add I don't have a sovereign opinion concerning this, but I do take into consideration the Badinter Commission and their arbitration on the self-determination of Serbs in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, that here self-determination cannot be envisaged in the sense of an independent state but that within the Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, they must have their rights that are due to them and that the borders should not be changed at the time -- those borders proclaimed at the time of independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you'll wait there, please, Professor, you will be asked further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you will bear in mind in asking questions that we have excluded this witness's evidence about autonomy in Kosovo and we have excluded the part of his report which deals with those matters, so therefore, no questions on those topics will be permitted. However, you may ask him, of course, about the rest of his report, about the position under the various constitutions about which he's given evidence further this morning. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, the witness spoke about this although you have excluded that subject, that is the autonomy of Kosovo. So if you really did not wish to have any of that mentioned, then you should have cautioned Mr. Nice so as not to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have. We have dealt with that. There is no evidence in relation to that unless you want to deal with a factual matter, which you can, but no other matter. I suggest you deal with other matters in relation to him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I shall deal with factual issues but also some questions that you say have been excluded but which do not necessarily have to pertain to the autonomy of Kosovo. They can reflect the reliability of the witness in this respect and in respect of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you're going to talk about his role in the Constitutional Court, you can. Of course you can ask him about that. But bear in mind we've excluded his opinion about the autonomy for that very reason; because he was involved. Also, you will have to show what it is that you challenge in his evidence. If you're going to question his credibility, you will have to show why it's necessary to do it. But go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kristan, you said a few minutes ago, when speaking about your career, that you were dean of the faculty of law, that you are a professor of law. So in addition to the fact that you were a Judge on the Constitutional Court, you were also involved in the science of law. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that the positions you presented in professional articles and other texts were based on professional arguments and the rules of the profession as such. Is that right, Mr. Kristan?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes. On the basis of my knowledge, of course, level of knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you did not adjust this to political needs and necessities. You abided by the rules of the profession, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: That was certainly my intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this professional opinion, expert opinion that we got and that you made, this is rather a voluminous paper. You did this at the request of Mr. Nice, or, rather, his side. Did you also compile that strictly abiding by the rules of the profession, avoiding political requirements possibly?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: That was certainly my intention. And if you have any doubts in connection with that, I would ask you to quote the area where you have a doubt, such a doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that too, not to worry, Mr. Kristan. So as you said yourself, you dealt with this exclusively on the basis of professional rules and law. That means that your positions should have been stable, that they should not have changed.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes. That's the logic of it. Depending on the time and the scope when I presented my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. That is why I'm referring to stability, because professional and scholarly criteria, I assume, are rather inflexible in this regard. Do you believe that this scientific scholarly objectivity makes you eligible to testify about such matters that you are testifying about now, as a matter of fact? And does this give you a certain credibility for constitutional legal matters? Is that right, Mr. Kristan?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And now, please, let us use a concrete example to verify the stability of your positions and also your professional criteria and reliability. I'm going to quote a few sentences from an article of yours. I'm going to ask you whether it was political reasons and necessities that led to the content of what you wrote then, and could you please confirm to me whether your positions presented then remain stable or, rather, whether you still espouse these views. Mr. Kristan, this is your very own text, one that I have in front of me. In volume number 10 of the periodical Socijalizam from 1981, you published an article, and I assume that you recall it. It deals with the constitutional legal position, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you recall the article, Dr. Kristan, at least in general terms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do remember that -- this article, but of course I would wish to see the area quoted, the paragraph quoted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. You can ask the question, and if necessary -- just a moment. Then the witness will be able to see the article you're quoting from over the adjournment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'll certainly let him have a look, but I need this for a few quotations. I need to have it with me, because I have it highlighted here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is on page 1731, Mr. Kristan. And may I tell you, gentlemen, that this periodical has pages of its own regardless of the numbers. So that is why there is such a large number of pages involved. The pages started from the first issue of that periodical, actually. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. What you wrote here is as follows. I'm just going to quote a section from here. You talk about the untenability of the position that was then held by Albanian separatists, and you say: "When Dr. Hajrudin Hoxha assessed the contribution of constitutional amendments from 1968 to the equal positions of the nations and nationalities of Yugoslavia, he pointed out that not in a single state where he followed the position of national minorities he did not find such positive treatment of national minorities as was the case in Yugoslavia." And then you say further on: "Dr. Hajrudin Hoxha, Professor of the Pristina University repeated this position even more decisively this year after the irredentist demonstrations broke out in Kosovo". And then you quote him. You say: I have visited over 60 countries. I attended various international gatherings organised about this subject over the past several years, and I came to a conclusion that no one can refute, not a single national minority did not attain the kind of rights that the Albanian national minority attained in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The Albanian nationality has the same right like any nation. I should just like to mention that it's only Hungarians in Romania and Swedes in Finland that enjoy such rights and so on and so forth. And then you say in relation to the claims that Albanians in Yugoslavia should have a republic of their own rather than only autonomy so that they could become allegedly equal. Now these are your words: "The slogan Kosovo Republic, the way the Albanian contra-propaganda put it is counter-revolutionary, hostile because its aim is to change the constitutional order of Yugoslavia, to change its constitutional borders, and finally to realise annexation of Kosovo to Albania." That is what you wrote yourself, Mr. Kristan. Now, tell me, do you believe today as well that before the constitution of 1974, inter alia thanks to the constitutional position of the autonomous provinces, the nationalities or, rather, the ethnic minorities in Serbia had an incomparably better position than anywhere else in the world?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just deal with that very briefly, and then, Dr. Kristan, we will give you the opportunity to read the article before you're required to answer any more questions about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to consult this quotation. I do remember this article, and it referred to the justification or not of the slogan "Kosovo Republika." At the time, as I remember it now, I was advocating the position that here a solution should be found in the sense of an autonomy, not in the form of a republic, because self-determination which was proclaimed at the second session of Avnoj in 1943, self-determination was considered the right of nations to organise themselves into states, while for ethnic minorities autonomy was envisaged and ensured. And this was a part of the constitution. And this referred -- applied to Vojvodina and Kosovo. They were not organised as republics but as two autonomous provinces. And it is from this point of view I -- which I hold today is for ethnic minorities is that autonomy is viable. And this is also the position of the Badinter arbitration committee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. It's now time to adjourn. Mr. Milosevic, show -- let the witness have the copy of that article so he can read it over the adjournment and save us time. Yes, if the usher would get a copy of the article.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask the registrar if she would be so kind as to make a photocopy and give Mr. Kristan that photocopy. It's not too long. And then could I have this particular copy returned to me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We will do that if the registrar would arrange for the copy to be made. Dr. Kristan, we're going to adjourn now for 20 minutes. During that adjournment, you'll have a chance to look at the article. Would you remember, please, and we have to warn all witnesses formally of this, not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. Could you be back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Dr. Kristan, you've now had the chance of reading that article. Is there anything you want to add to your previous answer to clarify your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have already mentioned, one should take the whole article and its meaning which was written in 1981 on the basis of the then knowledge that I had and the fact that we had at our disposal concerning the protection of the rights of ethnic minority in Kosovo. One has to bear in mind that the constitution of 1974, compared to other constitutions, protected very highly the ethnic minorities. But it doesn't mean that it also applied to the ethnic Albanians in Kosovo. And my article did not accept the thesis Kosovo Republic, because it would imply the disintegration of Yugoslavia, and also because it was against the decisions of the second session of Avnoj where some bases were constructed for the future Yugoslavia, the right to self-determination of the nations, and the status of ethnic minorities was defined. Later, my understanding was broadened concerning the status of the ethnic Albanians in Kosovo, and later in the Constitutional Court in 1989, I initiated a procedure concerning the law on internal relations in Kosovo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Doctor, those are two matters which we have excluded evidence about. Thank you. Yes. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. I just wish to add that later I determined that a lot of injustice was being made to the ethnic Albanians in Kosovo. We had the facts, and I remember Josip Ferhovic [phoen] and the discussion with him, namely members of ethnic Albanians were being detained without any right of defence, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The effect of it was, you say, that that was your understanding at the time you wrote the article but you received more information and found out other things which would lead you to hold different views subsequently. Would that be a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, that would be a summary. But already then, I advocated the position that it's not acceptable, this demand for a Kosovo republic because it was against the Avnoj decisions and against the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Kristan. Is it correct to say that the status of autonomous provinces in Serbia, according to the 1974 constitution, far existed -- exceeded the notion of autonomy and was in fact very close to the status enjoyed by the republics themselves?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Formally, as I have already mentioned, the status of autonomous provinces was close to the status of republics, but formally they remained at the level of autonomies and they never had the right to form their own states. In my report, I attempted to indicate that this formal status was deteriorating concerning Albanians in Kosovo. This deterioration began with the constitutional amendments in 1989 and the laws in 1989 referred to concrete relations when some bodies and companies were disbanded, were released, and special circumstances were introduced. Then the Assembly of Kosovo were -- had to stop working, the Presidency, and all these were concrete facts which led to the deterioration of the protection of the Albanian nation -- nationality in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You say on page 1731 of this article of yours, since you have it in front of you, it is paragraph 4 on page 1731, you say that claims that the Albanians in Yugoslavia were unequal, that they were nationally in jeopardy, could only be described as an example of hostile nationalist propaganda. Introducing parity and the decision-making in the Federation equates the position of provinces with the republics. That was your position then. Isn't at that right, Mr. Kristan?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: I quoted here a secondary source which was quoting this assessment, and I didn't go into that further. This was a conclusion for me. And my position was that this does not imply the right to proclaim Kosovo a republic and its severing from Yugoslavia, which on the basis of the fact we -- facts we had in Yugoslavia was the interests of Albania. And probably this interest existed at the time. And with that intention, I did not agree on the basis of the right to self-determination of a nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And you say in paragraph 3 on this same page which I'm mentioning, the question of inequality of Albanians - that the word "inequality" by you is placed in quotation marks - in Yugoslavia and Kosovo should be viewed from two standpoints, first from the factual truth and secondly from the point of view of the consequences should the Albanians have a different status regarding the other nations and nationalities of Yugoslavia. Is that still your opinion as you wrote about the Albanian separatist movement and its demands in 1981?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: I still believe so, but the emphasis is on the true state of affairs. What was the state of affairs in 1981. I quoted here secondary sources what the situation was. But the understanding of the true state of affairs I later on -- I also quote later on, that such matters should be further elaborated as far as a possible, different organisational setup in Kosovo as the Albanians were a majority in Kosovo. They were not their minority. They had to have a different access to the various organs, and they were subordinated to the Serbian minority there. And that was, I believe, also the reason why Albanians requested a republic and not a formal basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... claiming, Mr. Kristan, that when you wrote this in 1981 after the revolt of 1980, that the Albanians were not equal in Kosovo because they were under the authority of the Serbian minority in Kosovo? Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: I assert that this comes out of a more detailed analysis, later analysis of the relationships prevailing in Serbia, i.e., Kosovo. Explicitly you could see that with the proclamation of the special circumstances in Kosovo in February 1989 when the Kosovo Assembly was forced to accept a change of the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Serbia and of all the measures which were adopted by the Serbian Assembly against Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We won't go into this, whether the Assembly was forced or not, and that is not a constitutional legal question. But on this same page, you enumerate a number of facts, and then you say those facts elucidate everything but rather than the exploitation of the Albanian nationality in Kosovo. That is what you say. It is indicative of everything other than national exploitation.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: I have to repeat it -- you're repeating page 31, but I reiterate; this is a secondary source. I quote this source, and the emphasis is of an analysis and assessment of the true state of affairs which turned out to be untrue. There was a gap between the formal status and the de facto status between the Albanian nationality -- concerning the Albanian nationality. And it didn't have the rights guarantee which formally belonged to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Doesn't what you say applies to the formal and the de facto? On page 2 you say this comes to expression in the slogan Kosovo Republic and nationalist propaganda coming from Albania in support of that slogan. Albanian propaganda states the equality of Albanians in Kosovo as being the main argument, and you quote, in favour of the justified demand for Kosovo to gain the position of a republic. And you refer to Zeri i Popullit, the Albanian newspaper, which says that the Albanians in Yugoslavia do not have the rights that should be theirs for which they shed blood, and there was a chauvinist policy being pursued, and you attack these views as nationalist propaganda.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, be more precise. Look at the individual parts of the article are all parts of a whole. We know what later on turned out to be the Albanian interest. I consider it on the next page, whether this interest of Albania existed, whether it encouraged this demand of Kosovo Republic and the secession of Kosovo which would merge with Albania. This is a different level in -- state level interest. So this had to be attacked as an acceptable propaganda, and I see nothing negative in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course you don't see anything wrong with that. It was nationalist propaganda indeed, and that is what I wish to assert. Look at page 1733, please. You illustrate here their slogans "We want a republic by force or by will," and all these slogans are directly aimed at other nations and nationalities, especially the Serbs, Montenegrins and Turks. The slogan on Kosovo Republic is equally dangerous as the slogan on the annexation of that republic to parts of Macedonia and Montenegro inhabited by Albanians. And the attack on the constitutional order is only the first step towards jeopardising the integrity and constitutional order of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes. And later on -- obviously you should go on reading this article, because later on I do say and emphasise that the counting of membership of a nation can be fatal for the ethnically mixed territory of Yugoslavia. And this is what you can find in page -- on page 1734 and also what Raja Vasiliw [phoen] says, emphasising the riskiness, the danger of using such words and slogans. And it is in this respect that it is unacceptable that one part on such a territory should want to proclaim its independence. In these terms, this requirement, this demand is unacceptable. And then on page 35 I do stress that more understanding and also consensual settling of these questions on Kosovo is what is called for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I agree with you, Mr. Kristan, regarding what you wrote in 1981. The problem is that you don't appear to agree with yourself, or rather, with the position you held at the time. So please, as I quoted a moment ago, quite a concrete issue, that is an ethnically pure Kosovo, et cetera, that you mention, my question is, and I wish to remind you of these things and I'm sure that, a serious person, you will give very close thought to this: The expressions "an ethnically pure," "ethnic cleansing," was that expression first used --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have now spent the best part of half an hour on an article which the witness wrote 22 years ago in the circumstances of the time, as he has explained. His evidence which he's given today and his report concern the constitutional issues, particularly the powers of the president of Serbia, which is relevant to this indictment. 1981 was long before the indictment period. Now, you must move on to something else, Mr. Milosevic, because time, as you know, is limited. This witness cannot be here longer than today. Your time, therefore, must take account of that. Now, I cannot see any relevance at all, as far as this witness is concerned, about events in Kosovo at the time that you're dealing with. So you must move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those events, Mr. May, continued later on. I asked Mr. Kristan whether the expressions "an ethnically pure" and "ethnic cleansing" first started to be used in Yugoslavia precisely in connection with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Irrelevant as far as his evidence is concerned. He's giving evidence about the constitutional position.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely about constitutional matters, because these terms first started to be used, that is ethnic cleansing of Serbs and other non-Albanians, and the perpetrators were the Albanian separatists. That's what Mr. Kristan speaks about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No doubt those are matters we shall have to rule upon in due course, but for the moment, this evidence is not appropriate from Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kristan, in a broader sense and not just with respect to Kosovo, on page 34, at the end of that page, you say that the slogan of "Kosovo as a Republic" is in contradiction with the foundations of the Yugoslav Federation which is based on the equality of nations and nationalities of Yugoslavia. And this is one of the main achievements of the national liberation struggle and revolution, and its substance is not to separate nations and nationalities but to associate them, to strengthen their community in this territory. And then you go on to say that is why Josip Broz Tito said the Federation doesn't mean drawing borders between federal units and then for each of them to work at will regardless of others. And then you quote that the borders of federal units in federal Yugoslavia were not borders of separation but borders of unification. Is that right, Mr. Kristan?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Well, this is the meaning that can be deduced from my writing, namely it is necessary to achieve a consensual solution of all the relationships within the existing concept of the Federation which was established at the second session of Avnoj, i.e., the principle of self-determination and recognition of autonomy to national minorities. And this is in the interest of preserving Yugoslavia such as it was established after the end of the national liberation war, according to the constitution of 1964 to 1974. Tito was the one who drew the attention to the central issue of existence of Yugoslavia. And if you are referring to Tito's position, then I believe it is necessary to refer also to his position that it was necessary to respect not only formally but also in concrete relations the equality of nations and nationalities. The merit of Tito is that the new Yugoslavia, i.e., the second Yugoslavia which was conceived in 1943, became different than was the former Kingdom of Yugoslavia which was a unitary state and where the principle of equality of peoples and nations was not applied. Some nations. But not even mentioned, not to speak recognised. For example, the Montenegrins were not mentioned. Macedonians were not recognised. Only the Federation created by Tito gave an equal footing to all these nations. So they were all equal subjects at that time. Then the Montenegrins again obtained their statehood which was taken away from them in 1918 when the King Nikola was toppled and when Montenegro was merged with Serbia. This was Tito's historical role, and I -- when quoting Tito, I believe that in line with his positions and with his active policies we can find the struggle for equality of all nations and nationalities including the Albanians in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just one minor correction, Mr. Kristan. I quoted him from your own text, so I didn't quote him from anywhere else but from a text you yourself wrote when you said borders were linking people rather than separating them. You also say something which I think has principled meaning or substantive meaning for subsequent events. Also on this page 34, you say: "Any such national counting and regrouping is particularly fatal for nationally mixed territories such as these provinces are. Pressures are brought to bear on other nations and nationalities; chauvinist incidents going as far as certain members of nations and nationalities having to move out because of the feeling of jeopardy. This has been happening for a long time in Kosovo from which a large number of Serbs and Montenegrins have already moved out. So according to the 1981 census as compared to the 1971 census, members of these two nations are less numerous and not only in relative terms." And then you say: "In 1971 there was 18.3 per cent Serbs and Montenegrins 2.5 per cent, whereas in 1981 there were only 13.2 or 1.7 respectively. They are less numerous in absolute numbers of Serbs 8.1, Montenegrins 4.8, whereas the number of Albanians at the same time went up by 34 per cent." And then you say: "See tables regarding the national composition of Serbia and Kosovo published in Jovan Rajicevic's paper. What is the meaning of the slogan Kosovo Republic?" So you refer to this other author. So this counting the nationality members and exodus under pressure that you referred to here, that is on the part of Serbs and Montenegrins in large numbers from Kosovo. Isn't that right, Mr. Kristan? That is what you yourself wrote about.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Well, I must say I wouldn't like to re-interpret these statistics. I did not study these statistics in detail. I quoted them as a secondary source. With regard to the fact that slogan Kosovo Republika and its implementation are not acceptable, it is from this angle that I am dealing with this issue. This slogan is not acceptable. For this reason I criticise also the interference of Albania and its interest in instigating this counting and regrouping of the members of Albanian minority with the potential possibility of secession and merging with Albania. It is from this angle that I am quoting this as unacceptable. But the fact remains that it would be necessary to -- as far as the statistics are concerned, it would be necessary to study the statistics concerning the structure of the population in Kosovo for further needs. It would also be necessary to see what is the attitude of the Albanian nationality in Kosovo vis-a-vis the remaining part of the population. I believe that the percentage right now is around 90 per cent. And what was the representation, the rate of representation of the Albanians in the bodies of the Republic of Serbia? I believe that this is the problem that should be studied with regard to these statistics, because in real life it became evident that the Albanians were under-represented and could not cope, decide about issues in Serbia and that this was the reason for their dissatisfaction and for the slogan Kosovo Republic, because they believed that if they were a republic, their position would have been different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but precisely in relation to what you've mentioned just now in this article of yours, you say: "The irredentist tendencies of the Albanian nationalists in Kosovo are not a recent phenomenon. They actually appear as an extension of various quisling and fascist organisations that fought during the war against the National Liberation Movement of the Yugoslav peoples and against the achievements of the revolution." Is that right, Mr. Kristan?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I make the obvious point that we are well outside the area of the witness's expertise and it will be regrettable in the extreme if the accused finds himself at half past one saying he hasn't had time to deal with the witness or whatever time limit we may reach. He should frankly deal with matters of law. These matters of composition of Kosovo can probably be taken from the article and put to the demographer when the demographer is called in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, I was consulting as to time. You've only got, as you know, we only have the witness here today, so you've only got that time. You're choosing to spend it on this article and Kosovo and choosing it, in my judgement, to be spending it not wisely. Just a moment. The time that you will have will be all but the last half hour, unless Mr. Tapuskovic is prepared to give up some of his time to you. But it will, of course, depend on how you choose to spend the rest of that time whether it's right that you should get some extra or not. Mr. Tapuskovic, how long do you anticipate being, at the moment, with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is really hard for me to judge at this point in time, but as for the time that is left for me, I will try to deal with those questions that I can deal with within a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. I think that this is quite clear what Mr. Nice said, that the point that is being made is of a demographical nature. That is not true. The point is quite different. I think that this can be seen from Mr. Kristan's article. It is not demography.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kristan, let us go back to the constitutional subject matter that you are predominantly testifying about. It is not disputed on the basis of what you wrote then that Albanian separatists attacked the constitutional order and the integrity of the country. From a constitutional point of view, do you think that the Republic of Serbia had the obligation to protect the basic rights of its citizens throughout the territory of the republic? Did the Republic of Serbia have the obligation to protect the territorial integrity of the republic guaranteed not only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must have a question and not a series like this. You were asked whether there was this obligation on the Republic of Serbia to protect the basic rights of its citizens. Would you agree with that, Dr. Kristan?
