utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Serbia did have that obligation. On other hand, the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia had the same obligation, the safeguarding of the integrity of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So I assume that you're not going to challenge that Article 5, paragraph 2 of the constitution of the SFRY, that the territorial integrity is guaranteed by Articles 5 and 3 of the constitution of the SFRY? Isn't that right? Protection of the integrity of the republic and Yugoslavia, which is defined in the constitution of the republic, and in the constitution of the SFRY in these Articles and paragraphs of the constitution of the SFRY which I also mentioned to you. Is that right, Mr. Kristan?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Integrity has been guaranteed and the state is -- has the obligation to safeguard the integrity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as Serbia is concerned and as far as Yugoslavia is concerned. Is that right, Mr. Kristan?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: In all areas of the state with appropriate means and not in a general manner with some general actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: With appropriate means. Well, you do remember that the Presidency of the SFRY had passed decisions to have certain measures taken as far back as then, 1980 and 1981. You mentioned some of that too. You do recall that, don't you, I assume? All republics took part in the implementation of these measures. Is that right, Mr. Kristan?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Well, I do not remember this. I was not working on that. I didn't do any analysis. But I believe that for the later situation, that is for the crisis which emerged in Yugoslavia in 1986 and which culminated in 1989 when on the 27th of March, 1989, the Presidency of Yugoslavia proclaimed the state of emergency in Kosovo. Well, this is a new situation. This is not 1980. This is not 1981, and therefore, I believe it is impossible to link the two. The crisis of Yugoslavia was the crisis that occurred later. And this was the crisis that needed to be resolved, and then it became obvious that all the means which were tried to be used were unsuccessful, failed. Also, because of the policies led by Serbia and also due to the accused Mr. Milosevic who had his positions at that time, and he was in a position to implement his stance not only in the framework of Serbia but in the framework of Yugoslavia as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Kristan. As far as I can understand, you are testifying here about constitutional legal matters, not about my positions. Of course, as far as my positions are concerned, my conscience is clear. Mr. Kristan --

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Well, if you allow me, I'll explain myself. What was I referring to? I was referring to the events of 1989 with regards to the session of the Presidency of Yugoslavia of the 15th of March, 1991. At that time, the president, Jovic, tendered his resignation, and then you gave a special statement for the Yugoslav media where you deny your obedience to the Presidency and you also said that Serbia would not implement any decision of the Presidency of Yugoslavia. At that time, you didn't have any such powers, but you demanded from the Assembly of Serbia to dismiss a member of the Presidency of Yugoslavia. This was not one of your constitutional powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As for my constitutional powers, they include presenting proposals, suggestions, et cetera, and this decision was passed by the competent authority, that is to say by the Assembly of Serbia. You, as a constitutional lawyer, would have to know that. As for Jovic's resignation, our insistence was that he should return, and he did indeed return after a decision passed by the Assembly of Serbia that he should return and that he should continue discharging his duties at the Presidency of the SFRY. If you remember all of that, and I assume you do, Mr. Kristan.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: I do remember. I do remember. However, I also remember - and I have to correct you - it wasn't your -- under your constitutional powers to request the Assembly of Serbia to recall the member of the SFRY Presidency from Kosovo, Sapundziu, because the Assembly of Serbia was not, I say not empowered to recall him, and here you intervened erroneously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's going to be easy for us to debate that issue, because even citizens can present proposals, according to our laws, let alone the president. And this also has to do with decisions of the National Assembly of Serbia. So this cannot be challenged. Now, your expert opinion that you presented here pertains to the SFRY constitution, to the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the constitution of the Republic of Serbia. Is that right, Mr. Kristan?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes. I also touch upon the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and I wonder what is contradictory that you find.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you've been called to testify here, and in this room here, there are persons who, although lawyers, were trained in different legal systems, and by the very nature of things, they cannot know or they cannot know very well about the subject matter that you are testifying about and that is why you have been called as a witness. That is what I assume. And you are giving this expert opinion about these three constitutions. Since you are a scholar, the number of published works, articles, et cetera, is a touchstone for one's professional references. Tell me, how many such works did you published in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: I don't believe this is relevant. I was -- I'm a law professor, and I wrote textbooks on the constitution, constitutional law, a group of authors, Professor Ribicic, Professor Grad [phoen], Professor Kapcic [phoen], and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you published an article about the constitution of Yugoslavia. You published this particular paper professionally?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes. Articles were published. It would be difficult for me to enumerate all of that. I think that you have a list of my articles and my professional biography, a list of articles in English and German.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you write any articles about the constitution of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: No specific article. But for this occasion, I went through the constitution of Yugoslavia, and on the basis of that I submitted my views and which you can find from 75 onwards. And where I touched upon particularly on the proclamation of the constitution and I question the correctness of the procedure itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since you did not write anything about the constitution of Serbia, as you said yourself, that actually means that in this field, as far as the constitution of Serbia is concerned, there is no difference between you and the other lawyers sitting in this room because you never really dealt with this. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. That's not a fair point. The fact that a scholar doesn't write on a particular subject doesn't mean that he's perfectly competent to write about it. Now, this witness is a constitutional lawyer with knowledge of the Yugoslav constitutions, and that has been his evidence, and we've got his curriculum vitae. So let's move on. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kristan, a significant portion of your expert opinion pertains to the relationship between the constitution of the SFRY and the constitution of Serbia and the powers of the members of the Presidency and the Presidency as such in the field of national defence and also the powers of the republics; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes. A certain part of it is. Here the question is raised concerning the relationship and the attitude towards the SFRY constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since you're testifying under oath and you have the obligation to tell the truth, why did you keep silent about Chapter 8 of the constitution of Serbia which is entitled "Attitude Towards the Constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia"?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: I don't know what in concrete terms are you referring to. I believe --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In concrete terms, in that chapter of the constitution of the Republic of Serbia, there is Article 135. There was a great deal of debate with regard to this and it is impossible for an expert in this field not to know about its substance and that particular paragraph. My question is: Why did you remain silent about that particular chapter and that particular article? Please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Why should he have commented on it? What is the point you're making, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. May, the existence of that chapter and that article in the constitution of Serbia and the fact that it was left out of the expert opinion disfigures the constitution of Serbia in many important aspects.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, in what way? Just explain what you mean.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to do that right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kristan, the constitution of the Republic of Serbia was adopted on the 28th of September, 1990; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And at that time, the authorities of the Republic of Slovenia, the Republic of Croatia had already expressed their intentions to secede from the SFRY. They had already taken the first steps in that direction. For example, on the 1st of July, the Assembly of Slovenia adopted a resolution on the sovereignty of Slovenia. In April and May, when the HDZ came to power, their programme also envisaged the creation of a sovereign state of Croatia; isn't that right? Is that undisputed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: These events weren't completely synchronised, and I wonder how Mr. Milosevic interprets the Article 135 for which he wants to hear my interpretation. And I'd like -- why does he connect Slovenia and Croatia with this? They were already on the way to independence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment. Dr. Kristan, don't, if you can avoid getting into an argument with the accused because otherwise time will be taken up. Everybody is in the dark as to what the point is that you're making. Now, if you've got a serious point and a concrete point about this article, make it, but otherwise, let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Nice, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One of the relevant documents is listed in the list of exhibits. It's one of the exhibits already listed. It's P132. I think there were some courtesy copies in court but I'm not sure how many are available. If you want to find it ... And perhaps one can go to the witness as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Milosevic, while we're getting a copy of that, if you'd like to move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is very important, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In such a situation, I mentioned that before the constitution was adopted, there was already the declaration of Slovenia and the express desire on the part of Croatia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. What is this? I've been given an enormous bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't intend that you have the whole bundle. This is all the previous exhibits that might sensibly be referred to. It's the second of those. It's marked as P132. It's the second one down and that's all you require. And it's actually the last page of that. It's page 57 of that exhibit, as numbered. And the witness should be provided with a copy of the original, which can be found on the top right-hand corner on page 28 of 36.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed, Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We now have the article.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Chapter 8 says Relationship to the Constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Article 135 reads as follows: "The rights and duties vested under the present constitution in the Republic of Serbia, which is part of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, violate the equal terms of the federal constitution are to be exercised in the Federation shall be enforced in accordance with the legal constitution." So Mr. Kristan, is it clear that Serbia when it passes a constitution on the 28th of September, 1990, when other republics had already announced that they would leave Yugoslavia altogether, it does not want to have any kind of legal vacuum left behind, but it considers all of these provisions that pertain to the subject matter that you've been dealing with here, that they are not being carried out in conformity with that constitution but that they're actually being carried out in conformity with the federal constitution.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: This is a provision which, as I understand what Mr. Milosevic stated, with which it was wished to cover up the fact that the Republic of Serbia essentially changed the constitution of Yugoslavia in the sense that it abolished the status of autonomous provinces which were a creation of the constitution of Yugoslavia. Now, if we quote the first paragraph of Article 135, that the Republic of Serbia will be performing on the basis of the federal constitution, that's not true. You've eliminated, you've abolished the rights of the autonomous provinces which were enlisted in the federal constitution. You've abolished their constitution. You've took from them -- you abolished the Assembly as a legislative body and the Presidency which was compulsory according to the federal constitution. You've abolished the constitutional court there, all of that which was envisaged in the previous order. So this first paragraph does not meet that what was happening. These rights were not being exercised any more, and they did not exist in the constitution of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I am not understanding this. The English version of Article 135 doesn't read well. I'd like to ask the interpreter to translate the version in the B/C/S language.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have a copy of any text in any language. We are sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Could they be provided with a text. They can have one of ours, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, Mr. Kristan is talking about some special rights in terms of national defence. It is true that the constitution of the Republic of Serbia does contain such provisions in order to avoid the possibility of a legal vacuum, because before that both Slovenia and Croatia had announced their secession. However, Article 135, both de jure and de facto deals with the rights that the Republic of Serbia has in accordance with this constitution. That is what it says, the rights and responsibilities that Serbia has in accordance with this constitution and which according to the federal constitution are being exercised and the Federation shall be carried out in accordance with the federal constitution. That means that nothing that was envisaged as a power of the Republic of Serbia with regard to these issues that Mr. Kristan is testifying about, that is to say defence and so on and so forth, will not be carried out. This will be applied in accordance with the federal constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let us -- let us hear the translation of Article 135 so we can have a better understanding of it. The interpreters now have it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you give us an interpretation of Article 135.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Article 135 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first paragraph of Article 135. They can see it now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters will translate it as follows: "Article 135. The rights and duties that the Republic of Serbia which is within the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia has in accordance with this constitution and which according to the federal constitution shall be exercised within the Federation shall be carried out in accordance with the federal constitution." That is the end of the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It is totally different. That is more intelligible than what we have here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Then we can proceed, I hope, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could you conclude the interpretation. There is a second part to 135.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters shall now interpret the second paragraph. "When enactments of the agencies of the Federation or enactments of the agencies of another republic in contravention of the rights and responsibilities that it has in accordance with the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia infringe upon the equality of rights of the Republic of Serbia or in any other way jeopardise its interests and if no compensation has been provided for, the republican authorities shall adopt enactments in order to protect the interests of the Republic of Serbia." End of translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Milosevic, I think what you should now do is put very succinctly the significance of this article to the witness and the witness will comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Kristan, is it clear that everything you said in relation to national defence and the alleged responsibilities that are contained in the constitution was not being applied in accordance with the constitution of Serbia? Article 135, that is to say, these powers that according to the federal constitution are exercised within the Federation that will be carried out in accordance with the federal constitution. That is what is highlighted that these powers that are envisaged by the federal constitution will be carried out in accordance with the federal constitution. So everything that you explained in terms of some kind of powers of the authorities of Serbia in this domain has been eliminated altogether. This shall be exercised in accordance with the federal constitution. That is what Article 135 says.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: I wanted to draw the attention to the specific nature of this first paragraph, because each part of this first paragraph should be taken into consideration. We speak of the rights and duties of the republic of Serbia which is part of the Socialist Federal Republic, and on the basis of this constitution adopted on the 28th of September in 1990, these rights will be pursued in line with the federal constitution. The fact is that the -- this constitution of the Republic of Serbia does not have the institutions concerning the autonomous provinces and which still exist in the federal constitution. The Presidency, for example, of the autonomous province is linked to the federal organs, the Federal Presidency. That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kristan, what I am challenging from your testimony is the fact that you glossed silently over Article 135 has nothing to do with the provinces. It has to do with the competence of Serbia which you insisted upon, and if you had mentioned Article 135 from the constitution of Serbia, you would have seen that with respect to defence, the competencies belong to the organs envisaged by the constitution of Yugoslavia and are exercised as stipulated by that constitution. Then it would have been clear how it would have been possible to envisage the armed forces of Serbia and why such forces were never formed, in fact. So if you hadn't been silent about Article 135, it would become clear that in the area of defence, and I am now talking about defence, as for the autonomy of provinces we've already discussed that, but in the area of defence, the appropriate competencies are vested in the bodies envisaged by the constitution of Yugoslavia, and that is very clearly stated in Article 135 and are exercised accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have stopped you because the witness must have the chance to answer the point. Yes, Dr. Kristan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here we're dealing just with the segment of defence. I didn't mention Article 135. I didn't deem it relevant. But let me ask which part of my report is being disputed here. I see no connection and no reason with which you are questioning my report. The fact that I didn't quote that article is not a question of refuting my report. I think this article should be in detail explained. But in this constitution, you haven't regulated the essential elements of autonomy. This is what I stress in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kristan, virtually throughout the examination-in-chief, Mr. Nice devoted almost all his time to these charts, and all these charts and your examination-in-chief dealt mostly with the functions of defence and the relationships between the various Presidencies. There are certain incorrectness there too but I won't dwell on them, but all these charts relate to defence. And I'm saying that precisely because of the fact that you did not mention Article 135, one can see that those defence functions were never, in fact, established in the Republic of Serbia because in that area, the appropriate competencies belonged to the bodies stipulated by the constitution of Yugoslavia, and Article 135 says that what the constitution of Yugoslavia stipulates will be implemented in accordance with those stipulations. And that is the explanation why no armed forces of Serbia were ever formed, because for as long as SFRY existed, the constitution of SFRY was implemented.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Well -- well, it seems to me important to emphasise once again. I did not see where my positions are not correct. I would like you to quote which is the position that I expressed that you do not want and which is in conflict. You say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Rather than get into an argument about this, as you interpret Article 135, Dr. Kristan, what effect did it have on any of the defence provisions which you say were in the law on defence of Serbia, or indeed on the constitution? What bearing, if any, did Article 135 have on these matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I do not see any effect of this article, and this article would not make impossible the defence of Serbia. The concept of defence of Serbia and of Yugoslavia were very clear and clearly defined in the constitution. This was the concept of the armed forces. And we have already established what the position of the armed forces and of the Territorial Defence were, and this has no relation with Article 135, with the constitution. There is nothing that would be unclear. This article did not rehabilitate or deny the concept of defence. In my opinion, this article is conflictual because it does not spell out clearly something. Mr. Milosevic has approached me that I did not mention on purpose this article. This was not the case. But in this article, it is not clear that there are no longer the fundamental institutions which had been provided for by the constitution. Now, in this constitution, no reference is made to the relations between the member of the Presidency of Serbia vis-a-vis the Assembly in the past. In the constitution it was clearly defined that the member of the Presidency elected by the Assembly of Serbia was answerable to the Assembly, that he or she was bound to present their views to the Assembly. Now this provision was deleted. What was the purpose of that? There is no longer any Presidency of autonomous province, which means that the structure of the Federation has thus been impaired in the sense that it had been conceived previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kristan, we are not talking about the Presidencies of autonomous provinces, Mr. Kristan. You testified about alleged competencies with respect to national defence and I quoted to tell you that what is stipulated by the federal constitution to be exercised in the Federation will be exercised in accordance with the federal constitution. That is what Article 135 says, and that is why no armed forces of Serbia were ever formed, because that was within the competence of the Federation. And according to Article 135, what is the responsibility of the Federation is done by the Federation. And later on, when the FRY was established, it was the army of Yugoslavia again. So these competencies Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were realised in the Federation. That is why no armed forces of Serbia were ever formed. That is quite consistent and in accordance with Article 135 of the constitution, which says that what is in the competence of the Federation will be regulated in the Federation. Only if the whole country had broken down, if Serbia had become an independent and autonomous state, would those provisions be implemented because in that case there would be no federal state which regulates matters of defence by its own constitution. So that is the whole point, Mr. Kristan, and as a constitutional lawyer, you know that full well.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me it would be correct if Mr. Milosevic explained why the constitution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't bother. If he doesn't make his point plain, there is no point pursuing it. And as I say, we do not want an argument. Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Your point is not clear. Now, you can either try and make it again so it's clear or you can do something else, move on to another point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it clear, Mr. Kristan, that you're talking about certain independent competencies of Serbia in the realm of national defence in your expert report and now in the examination-in-chief as well and in commenting these charts shown to you by Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Well, I apologise to the President Mr. May for having asked this question. Because I wanted to know why Serbia in this constitution of 1990 left out the Territorial Defence which had been a constituent part of the armed forces of Yugoslavia in all republics, in all constitutions, and also in the previous constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but let's try and shorten this. Is it your point, Mr. Milosevic, that the reason there wasn't any mention of the armed forces in the constitution was because its governed by Article 135? Is that the point you're making?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The armed forces are mentioned in the constitution, but Article 135 says that the competencies envisaged or provided for by the federal constitution shall be exercised in the federal state. Therefore, whatever is mentioned in the Serbian constitution about armed forces will be implemented in accordance with the federal constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's subject to 135. That seems to be the point. Yes. But the witness was dealing with the Territorial Defence, and that was what his evidence was about. Now, have you got any other points on this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can also draw attention to certain other matters in that connection which are quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kristan, on the basis of the SFRY constitution, did the TO of Serbia remain under the Supreme Command of the Presidency of the SFRY and not the president of Serbia? Because according to the law on national defence of SFRY, the commanders of Territorial Defence of the republics and the commanders of the TOs of the autonomous provinces were accountable to the Presidency of the SFRY for their work regarding combat readiness, deployment of troops, institutions, control and command, et cetera. This is Article 113 and 115 of the law of national defence. 113 and 115. Therefore, in that sense, these charts of yours are not correct. What is correct is that each republic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness answer these points. Yes. Now, about Article 113 and 115.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is the law on all people's defence.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: This law on general people's defence was based on a concept of the armed forces of Yugoslavia, i.e., the army and the Territorial Defence. This is what the constitution of Serbia of 1991 did not have. This constitution of Serbia left out the Territorial Defence as an essential segment of that defence of the armed forces of Yugoslavia, and this is where I see the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't that problem eliminated automatically by the fact that questions of defence pursuant to Article 135 shall be implemented in accordance with the federal constitution? So thereby automatically the constitution of Serbia says that what is envisaged by the federal constitution is implemented according to that federal constitution. Isn't that clear?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Well, here I believe that the legislator should have been more specific, more precise. Whenever such articles are concerned, the article which is so important to Mr. Milosevic, here a delegation is foreseen from the decisions and from the provisions which are in the constitution. I believe that here we should have enumerated by virtue of these articles these and these acts and regulations will be applied. I believe that it should be stated very clearly what is considered as a -- as issue covered by Article 135 of the constitution, and this was not done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Even I who is not a teacher but simply a lawyer, I think understand that something is enumerated if it is an exception. But if it says here that the rights and duties, that means all rights and duties which the republic has pursuant to its constitution. Therefore, all rights and duties which according to the federal constitution are implemented in the Federation will be exercised in accordance with the federal constitution. And because this relates to all rights and duties, there is no need to enumerate anything specifically. Whatever is within the competencies of the federal constitution, the Republic of Serbia considers shall be regulated in accordance with that constitution. Why would if be necessary to enumerate all these things, for the Republic of Serbia to say that all those things shall be exercised in accordance with the federal constitution? That is why there is no enumeration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is the -- this is the last question we'll deal with before the adjournment. Yes. Do you have any comment you want to make, Dr. Kristan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, of course. I believe this deserves a comment because if you say "all," then we have to take into consideration the fact that Article 135 excludes those things which are regulated by the federal constitution and which do not figure in the constitution of the Republic of Serbia. One of these things is the Territorial Defence. In your constitution, you did not regulate the Territorial Defence, and now you are saying that competencies according to these things. But according to this constitution, you do not have the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. We're going to adjourn now. Twenty minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we go on, I would like to ask the OTP to produce an official translation of Article 135 in due course, even if we heard it from the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As far as I know, this is indeed an official translation, but I think we will re-submit this entire article obviously for a further reconsideration by the unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just finish off with this part of the examination. Mr. Kristan, according to what you've said about the changes in the regulations in Yugoslavia, you spoke about the armed forces of Yugoslavia, didn't you? Therefore, let us clear this up. The expression "armed forces," does it absorb or include the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes. In terms of the constitutional order of Federal Yugoslavia, yes, but not in terms of the Serbian constitution of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. If the armed forces does imply the Territorial Defence as well, does the constitution of Serbia mention the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Well, as a constitutional lawyer, we have to be accurate. The notion of armed forces is not clearly determined. A special law was announced in this area. However, it had not been adopted. The fact is that the Serbian constitution does not include Territorial Defence, which beforehand had been a part of the Serbian constitution on the basis of the concept of the Yugoslav constitution, federal constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You yourself have explained that in the laws of Yugoslavia, the term "armed forces" was used, which does include the Territorial Defence, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, if the constitution of Serbia mentions the armed forces, then surely that means that it has used the terminology used in Yugoslav regulations, which means that it implicitly includes the Territorial Defence. Isn't that clear?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: That is a fact. Later on, this was changed, but you said that I overlooked the Article 135, and I think that in these terms, I would like this to be clearly put. And to my mind, a great shortcoming of the Serbian constitution lies precisely there, in this area. And in relation to the former constitution of the Republic of Serbia, which now in this situation left out the Territorial Defence, that we find in all other constitutions. And an interesting element to me is to question why this was so. And since you compel me to interpret or to comment, rather, Article 135, I must say that I see a problem there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is the whole point. Since the federal legislation uses the term "armed forces," and that means the Territorial Defence included, the constitution of Serbia mentions the armed forces, but by article 135, as that is part of the competence of the Federation, it leaves it within the competence of the Federation, because it says clearly that everything envisaged in the constitution of the Federation should be exercised in accordance with the federal constitution. Haven't we cleared that up?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Article 135, however, does not mention the armed forces, whereas you are saying that this is an exception, this article. And to me as a lawyer, I think that this calls for an explanation so as to be able to arrive at such a conclusion that you are putting forward, namely that this is something that cannot be gathered on the basis of this article, and therefore, we can say that the segment of Territorial Defence is not included.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are the armed forces within the competence of the Federation in any constitution of the FRY and the SFRY? Just give me an answer as a constitutional lawyer. It is -- are they within the competence of the Federation?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes. As a constitutional lawyer, I wish to add that the constitution of the republic must respect and abide to the constitution of the Federation which the constitution of the Republic of Serbia did not do, and only later on the level of legislation, not on the level of constitution it organised Territorial Defence. And I question what is the reason for it. What is the purpose of a constitution if the first paragraph of Article 135 is the application and the execution of the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia? It is superior, and its execution is in fact stronger.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The emphasis here is on the fact that the Republic of Serbia respects the constitution of Yugoslavia, because it says that the rights of duties that are invested in Yugoslavia according to the constitution are exercised in accordance with the federal constitution, which is quite in contradiction with what you are saying and with the fact that you omitted to mention this Article 135. Now, let me move on. Is it true that when we were discussing the regulations on Territorial Defence that the Presidency of the SFRY appointed the commander of each of the Territorial Defences of each of the republics? Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes. That's based on the law on All People's Defence of Yugoslavia. And in this law, the competencies and responsibilities of the commanders of TOs of the republics were defined in this law on All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And they were accountable to the Presidency of Yugoslavia. Isn't that right, Mr. Kristan?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The Presidency of Yugoslavia. And later when changes occurred, this accountability shifted to the staff of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I assume you will agree with me that this chart, number one, is not correct insofar as it talks about the presidents of the republics and autonomous provinces, whereas according to the constitution of 1974, they were not presidents but, rather, presidencies of the republics and autonomous provinces. Isn't that right, according to the 1974 constitution? These bodies were the presidencies, republican and of the autonomous provinces; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Precisely so. That was my comment, but obviously there was no time to correct this error or lapses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Also, when you say SFRY Presidency in this large box, it says Supreme Command and then in brackets president of the Presidency equals Supreme Commander. That also is not correct, because the Supreme Commander, according to the 1974 constitution, was the Presidency and not the president. Isn't that right, Mr. Kristan?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: The Presidency of Yugoslavia was the Supreme Commander and the command and control of the armed forces, and it was exercised by the presidents of the Presidency on behalf of the -- he did it on behalf of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So we finally agreed on that. Now, please, in spite of the secession of Slovenia and Croatia and then Bosnia-Herzegovina and Macedonia, the Republic of Serbia continued to respect the order of the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Two republics remained within the common state. And then when in April 1992 the constitution of Yugoslavia was adopted, they also proclaimed their continuity with the SFRY constitution. This is what you refer to in Articles 154, 155 and 410 of your expert opinion. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes. It refers to the matter of continuity. However, concerning the proclamation of this continuity on -- by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, what was contradictory was already the proclamation, a proclamation by an organ which didn't have an authority to proclaim it. The question is what was the intention to be achieved vis-a-vis the international community. Mr. Milosevic speaks of secession of Slovenia and Croatia. No such secession took place. I think one has to be correct and take into account the true state of affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. The true state of affairs will certainly be taken into account but we don't have time now so I just want to discuss some details. You say that the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was promulgated at the meeting of the Federal Chamber. Do you remember that the parliaments of the Republics of Serbia and Montenegro were there too? Is that right? So the members of the Federal Chamber from these two republics and also the full Republican Assemblies of both Serbia and Montenegro. Isn't that right, Mr. Kristan? Just say yes or no and we can go on. We haven't got more time.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: I don't have a list of those attending. In the media the reporting was that the Federal Chamber proclaimed the constitution, but the Federal Chamber didn't exist in composition with all the republics but only MPs from Serbia and Montenegro participated. That was the numbers which I know. And the media reported the number of -- in attendance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is the part that pursued the continuity of Yugoslavia, Serbia and Montenegro. You're not going to claim that the MPs from Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina and Macedonia were supposed to be invited too, those that had left Yugoslavia? Were they supposed to vote on whether Serbia and Montenegro would continue to exist as the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia? Is that perhaps what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: What I wish to say is that this procedure wasn't legally correct and that it's not correct that this proclamation of continuity wasn't legally relevant, because these two republics, in line with international Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. law and on the basis of evaluation of the Badinter Commission, didn't have a right to the continuity of SFRY but all republics had it, and this is then resolved in the process of succession, and it would be fit and proper for the two republics if they proclaimed this constitution independently. They would -- could call -- call a constituent Assembly and involving the Assembly of SFRY was not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Kristan. All right, Mr. Kristan. As for Badinter's commission, we're going to ask Mr. Badinter about that himself. Let's go on. Are you claiming that the law on how republican authorities should act under special circumstances is contrary to the SFRY constitution? You in paragraph 24 of your expert opinion, you say that in accordance with Article 230 of the SFRY constitution - I'm quoting your sentence - the rights and responsibilities guaranteed by the SFRY constitution cannot be taken away or restricted. That is a quotation. And then you say it is only possible to do this in a state of war according to Article 317 of the constitution of the SFRY. Rather, amendment 91, paragraph 3 gives to the Presidency of the SFRY. Is that right? Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes. It's not possible because here we -- I have to explain where -- why I state this. It was the state of the Republic of Serbia who intervened with special extraordinary measures. I've given the -- anti-constitutional elements were discussed by the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia, and that is why I said that it's impossible on the basis of Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia to withdraw and suppress the rights and the self-management rights. And the Republic of Serbia couldn't intervene in this way with a simple law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. When you say that the session of the Constitutional Court was not actually completed, I would like to draw your attention to the Official Gazette, 87/90. This is a decision on assessing the validity of the constitutional declaration on Kosovo as an independent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, perhaps you can assist with this. It sounds as though we're heading into the area which we ruled against.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I was going to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. We've ruled against this. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the witness deals with it, so I wanted him to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You invoked Article 203 of the constitution, which says the rights and liberties guaranteed in this constitution cannot be taken away or restricted. That is a quotation. However, you kept silent about something else, just like about one Article 135, that is that there is paragraph 2 of this same article as well. So of the SFRY constitution, we are dealing with both paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us deal with one matter, because you continually repeat it, which is a bad forensic practice. You make a bad point and then go on repeating it continually. The witness should have the chance to deal with it so it's plain on the record. The accused alleges that you did not deal with Article 135, you overlooked it, and it appears that what he's saying is that you deliberately ignored it. Now, you should have the chance to deal with that. Did you do that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I didn't keep silent about it. I didn't want to keep silent about it. It didn't seem relevant to me. But I did look for literature and explanation for this procedure, but I found no trace of this Article 135, its meaning, its function as Mr. Milosevic spoke of it today. I was interested in getting as much material as possible about it. However, if Mr. Milosevic refutes my view on the inalienability and liberties which are guaranteed, I would like to ask him what articles he quotes and refutes my stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kristan, that's why I'm going beyond that. You also invoke 204, and you say -- I'm sorry. In paragraph 24 of your expert opinion, you say that according to Article 203 of the SFRY constitution, the rights and liberties guaranteed by the SFRY constitution could neither be suspended or limited. So I've just quoted you now. So in the mentioned sentence, you correctly invoked Article 203 of the SFRY constitution which says the rights and liberties guaranteed by this constitution cannot be suspended or limited. You quoted that correctly. However, there is also paragraph 2 of that same constitutional article, Mr. Kristan, and it reads as follows: The rights and liberties envisaged by this constitution shall not be used by anyone in order to undermine the basics of the self-management constitutional order of this constitution and also the violation of the constitutionally guaranteed rights of man and citizen and international cooperation fanning interracial hatred or instigating the commission of crimes. And these rights and liberties cannot be used in a way which would offend public morality. Full stop. And then the law provides under which conditions and under which situation using rights or, rather, abusing rights guaranteed by this constitution means that they should be withdrawn altogether. So this is what it says in this same article and you quoted paragraph 1 of that article only. Is it being disputed, Mr. Kristan, that this expression "the law determines," so that is to say either republican or federal law, and when it is -- that is what is meant. It's either or. But when the federal law is meant only, then that is stated specifically. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: I believe that this stand on the inviolability of rights and liberties I think must be respected within the framework of the federal constitution and only -- the only departures can be outlined by the federal legislator. And I quoted the -- and emphasised the inviolability of the self-management right. And I'd say it is specially protected, and with the special measures, the Republic of Serbia intervened in this area by suppressing the self-management rights of the great majority of this population. It refers to 250 enterprises. And that is why I emphasised the inviolability of these rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you quoted only paragraph 1 and you kept silent about paragraph 2, and I quoted it to you only a short while ago so I don't want to quote it again. Because it does say that this right is restricted if racial, religious, or other types of hatred are being fanned and that this is prescribed by law. Isn't that right, Mr. Kristan?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you did not mention a part of this article which is much longer than paragraph 1 of that article. Because it does not fit into what you are trying to persuade people of here by way of your expert opinion. I think that you did this intentionally.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Well, this -- these recriminations that I intentionally omitted this, and I believe Mr. Milosevic knows I do not do, and I know what my responsibility is. And what in our constitutional administrative law showed that the laws adopted by the Republic of Serbia vis-a-vis the autonomous province of Kosovo where it intervened in all relationships prevailing on that territory of Kosovo that it impinged upon the entire territory. This was stated by Professor Medjedovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. I'm not interested in that. Tell me as a former constitutional judge of the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia, isn't the court the only one that is competent to judge whether something is in accordance with the constitution or not. Is that right or is that is not right, Mr. Kristan?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Constitutional Court perhaps judge that what the Republic of Serbia did was unconstitutional or not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: No, it didn't state that because it didn't in the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the Constitutional Court did not do that. I'm not interested in private personal opinions. Let's move on. In paragraph 131 of your expert opinion you say that, "The right to self-determination, including the right to secession, was stipulated in the Basic Principles I of the SFRY constitution." And then you quote that: "The nations of Yugoslavia, proceeding from the right of every nation to self-determination," and so on and so forth joined in a free republic of working people the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No need to answer this. We've ruled this bit out. Yes. Move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Already in the next paragraph you say that some authors, especially from Serbia, like Professor Djordjevic and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Mr. Milosevic, you know that that has been ruled out. The relevant parts are 148 onwards. Page 40. And you've got by my calculation another ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kristan, in the normative part of the constitution of the SFRY, doesn't Article 5 say that the territory of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is one and it consists of the territories of the socialist republics? And also the border of the SFRY cannot be changed without agreement of all republics and autonomous provinces? Is that right, Mr. Kristan? Is that what the constitution says?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say, actually, that it is the people that decide about self-determination, but people are actually organised within a state constituted as people within their republics joined within the Federation. That is your assertion. Is it correct, Mr. Kristan, that at the moment when the Yugoslav peoples established the Yugoslav state after the First World War and during the Second World War, there were no republics in existence?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: I regret and I apologise. I would be interested in debating the issue of self-determination, but I see that there is no time for that, and Your Honours did not give me -- didn't allow me to go into that. But in fact, if we wish to highlight this issue, we would have to go back to 1918 when the first Yugoslavia was formed and then focus on second Yugoslavia, which was founded in 1943 -- it has its foundations in 1943. The first Yugoslavia collapsed because there wasn't equality among nations. Now, the third -- and if Your Honours allow me, we had a number of elements joining this country. And -- however, the process of proclamation of that state and constitution wasn't in the spirit of this unification. Now, at the time it was the Kingdom of Serbia. Then the other country, the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes. There the problem of nations was wasn't resolved. Then there was Vojvodina, then the Kingdom of Montenegro, and here some issues weren't resolved. Now, in view of the policy of Serbia led by President Pasic, they merged with Vojvodina and then Montenegro and the King Nikola was toppled. And with that, the new Yugoslavia, the second Yugoslavia, tried to resolve these issues through the concept of Federation in order to ensure the equality of all nations and nationalities irrespective of their numerical strengths. And that is why we have the parity principle in the main federal organs. And when the two provinces joined, they were also represented. And those were the goals of this Federation. Now, the constitution in 1974 brought this level -- this Federation to a level which became critical because Serbia wasn't satisfied with this concept. Here we should then continue the debate. But for me, the main issue is this discussion about the reorganisation of Federation was not carried on with peaceful means but what ensued was an armed conflict which was at the time initiated by Serbia. And Mr. Milosevic, I would say, was an important figure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a matter that your evidence goes into. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. But you allowed the witness to explain at length what is not the subject of this hearing and you deny me any such right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to state, Mr. Kristan, that this quotation of yours that I mentioned, that is to say the peoples of Yugoslavia constituted as peoples within their republics joined together, and you say that this is a falsehood and therefore a forgery.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: I don't understand your assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There were no republics when Yugoslavia was formed after the First World War and during the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: You mean in 1918. In 1918, they were not. But in 1943, the Serb process was initiated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Initiated but republics were not formed then. Let's go on. In many --

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: The statehood of individual republics within the nations was being developed gradually in different intensities among different nations. If you take the case of Slovenia in point, Slovenia in 1941 already formed its highest organ of authority, the National Liberation Committee, which was supposed to represent the Slovene nation. And at the meeting at Kocevje prior to the second session of Avnoj --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kristan, we are not talking about the Slovenian national committee now, please.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: I only wanted to answer your question, namely I'd like to point out that individual nations developed their statehood already prior to the second session of Avnoj. The second session of Avnoj, 29th of November, 1943, the delegations of the individual nations' peoples came with their authorisations concerning decisions to be taken there. Namely that a new Yugoslavia would be formed as a Federation and not a unitarian state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm afraid time is short.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kristan, I'm afraid there's not much time left. In your expert opinion, you say that the amendments to the constitution of Serbia in 1989 and the constitution of 1990, and you also say today during your live testimony that this is against the SFRY constitution and that this changed the positions, and you invoke the constitution of the SFRY, Article 4, referring to autonomous provinces. And you do not quote Article 4 of the SFRY constitution anywhere. You just invoke it. You say that in 1989, autonomous provinces were deprived of their constitutional position which was based on Article 4 and that the position of the autonomous provinces was not observed, and so on and so forth. I would like to quote to you article 4 of the SFRY constitution, and it reads as follows: The socialist autonomous province is an autonomous self-management, democratic, social political community based on the power and self-management of the working class and all working people within which the working people and citizens, the nations and nationalities have exercised their sovereign rights. And when this is in common interest, then the republics as a whole by the SFRY constitution established this within the republics as well. So this is what the constitution of Yugoslavia says. Had you quoted this article, it would have been clear that precisely in this last part of the sentence prescribes that it is precisely the constitution of Serbia that allocates responsibilities or, rather, that divides responsibilities between the Republic of Serbia and the autonomous provinces within the republic depending on whether this involves common interests or not. I quoted the constitution of Yugoslavia to you which Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. says when it is in the interest of the republic as a whole, then the constitution of the republic will determine this within the republic. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you allow that, Mr. President? May I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I quoted the entire concept of the constitution of Yugoslavia as far as the status of autonomous provinces is concerned. This logic is there, and from the very beginning it was clear that the autonomous provinces share their destiny within the Republic of Serbia. This was clear. And the constitution of Yugoslavia, however, provided for certain guarantees to the autonomous provinces that the Republic of Serbia with its legislation and with its constitution could not strip them of this status. And this is where the problem appears. The rights started to be diminished, the rights enjoyed by the autonomous provinces by 1990, on the basis of the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Serbia, which was based on this concept of Federation and where Article 4 of the constitution of Yugoslavia was also taken into consideration. I did quote some of the amendments passed by Serbia in 1989 by way of which the previous position of autonomous provinces is weakened. But this process continued and reached its climax with the constitution of 1990. Then all the essential elements of the autonomous provinces were abolished with the constitution of the Republic of Serbia. The elements that had existed before in the Yugoslav constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it at issue that it was in accordance with the constitution of Yugoslavia, Article 4, the Republic of Serbia is competent to divide competencies between the republic and the autonomous provinces within it guided by the fact whether they were of common interest or not. This is the last sentence of Article 4 which states this very clearly, that this is established in the republic with respect to the autonomous provinces. You didn't quote the key paragraph.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: I apologise. I do not have here the text of the federal constitution, and I can't find it right now. Maybe somebody could help me to find the relevant text. But I believe that as far as this article is concerned, we should take into consideration of the word "also" because I believe it is the order which is important. Who is older? Who is the first? Here the constitution of Yugoslavia defined the ground and the basis of these rules and status. For the autonomous provinces in Serbia, it is also the constitution of the Republic of Serbia which applies. But this does not necessarily apply that the constitution of the Republic of Serbia could strip off the provinces of the status that had been guaranteed by the Yugoslav constitution. This is the logic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Constitution of Serbia of 1990 September, that you quoted from, are there autonomous provinces, that is Vojvodina and Kosovo and Metohija? Do they exist, that is Vojvodina and Kosovo and Metohija in the 1990 constitution of Serbia, because you say they were abolished?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: The autonomous provinces such as they had been created with the constitution of Yugoslavia are abolished. The constitution of the Republic of Serbia has an Article 6 to which you are most probably referring, and it says that autonomous provinces Vojvodina, Kosovo and Metohija exist as forms of territorial autonomy. This is where the importance lies. I do not know whether you underestimate the terminology, the constitution of 1974.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is of marginal significance, it seems, but you've got two more questions, Mr. Milosevic, by which time you will have had well over two hours to cross-examine. Now, two more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After the adoption of the constitution of Serbia, did the autonomous provinces remain constituent parts of the Federation? Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Well, the autonomous provinces, yes. They continued as part of Yugoslavia. However, they were no longer units of political territorial autonomy, as for the concept of SFRY, because Serbia rescinded territorial autonomy in this constitution which is contrary to the federal constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... bodies after the constitutional amendments in Serbia in 1990 that you are talking about, were the provinces represented in the same way that they were before, as regulated by the constitution of Yugoslavia, and those same people by name and surname kept the positions they held prior to those constitutional changes in Serbia. Just take as an example your own Constitutional Court of which you were a member.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Well, indeed more or less the same people were and kept their positions. However, Serbia abolished the institutions that previously had existed in autonomous provinces, and that is the Assembly of the autonomous province. And this Assembly had a right and duty to elect a member to the Yugoslav Presidency, and you interfered in that, rescinding the autonomous status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kristan, that is not true that the Assemblies of the autonomous provinces were abolished. The Assembly of Kosovo and Metohija was suspended because of unconstitutional acts and the proclamation of a republic which means flagrant violation of the constitution of both Yugoslavia and Serbia. Did anyone abolish the Assembly of Vojvodina or the Presidency of Vojvodina before the changes were made to the constitution of Yugoslavia? Why are you talking about constitutional matters and mixing them up with political circumstances and the irredentist movement in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Answer that question because of the suggestion which is made and then we will hear from Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the fact is that Serbia interfered into the functioning of Yugoslavia. Well, first of all, at constitutional level, interfering thus with the functioning of the institutions of autonomous provinces. Furthermore, also it -- it abolished the Assembly after they ceased their activities, as it was put. And this is an unacceptable argument or reasoning, because the Assembly is a legal body in accordance with the federal law and constitution of Serbia has no right to interfere with this status. Second, the existence of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, the Assembly of Serbia first of all dismissed Sapundziu contrary to the constitution, because this did not lie within the competence of the Serbia, and appointing its own member of the Presidency, and this was not part its responsibilities or competencies either. And this decision about putting an end to the functioning of the Assembly as well as dismissing the member at the federal level. Well, all of these acts were in fact against the constitution or were unconstitutional and the Constitutional Court as well in fact was just about to -- was no longer really operational.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, can't I be allowed to ask a few more questions, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. No, Mr. Milosevic. You've had much more than your time already. We must bring this witness's evidence to a close. Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, I would like to ask you to focus on a few points only so that we try to explain to Their Honours a few more points from your report. In the examination-in-chief and throughout your testimony, you spoke about the competencies of the Presidency of SFRY according to the 1974 constitution, and also in paragraphs 202, 203, 204, 205, and 206 you spoke about the competencies of the president of Presidency of Serbia. This is to be found in your conclusions but I would like to draw your attention to what is stated in paragraph 202. I quote: "The President of the Presidency of the Republic of Serbia had no formal relationship with the SFRY Presidency member from Serbia." Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Emphasis here is on a formal relationship in the sense of either a subordinated or inferior position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please, if possible, answer clearly. This is what you explicitly stated. Do you abide by what you said?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Well, it's got to be also read together with what follows and what went on then, and it is clarified that the president of the Presidency then in fact acts as a substitute, and I've already explained this earlier on today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you literally to comment on what you said. I'm moving on to paragraph 203: "... a formal relationship did exist between the SFRY Presidency member from Serbia and the Assembly of Serbia..." That is what you wrote in your report. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: But this is not questionable in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I agree, and that's why I'm drawing your attention to it. And finally in paragraph 204, according to the 1974 constitution of Serbia and amendment so-and-so, the SFRY Presidency member from Serbia is answerable to the Assembly of Serbia and is obliged to report on the functioning of the SFRY Presidency to the Assembly. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes. But you also have to read on Article 205 or item 205 where it is -- we can see that a Serbian Republic left out this and the question is why.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm really asking you only with respect to what you wrote in your report, because according to the 1974 constitution, did the same apply with respect to the representative of any republic in the Presidency? That is, that that president was answerable to the Assembly of his republic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Well, the member from any republic is answerable to the Assembly from his or her republic or autonomous province, to their own Assembly --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: -- Serbia in the case of autonomous provinces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now, Mr. Nice showed you these four charts, one, two, three, four, which you prepared together with the Prosecution, and between these two boxes, that is the Presidency of the SFRY and their representatives, in between there we have the presidents of the republics and of the autonomous provinces. Isn't that wrong? Shouldn't we have there instead that the link between the SFRY Presidency and the republics was the Assembly and not the president of the republic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Well, it is not inaccurate, but I think it would be better to say that it is insufficient and it was a slip of the tongue. And then what is missing here is probably a first table illustrating a more comprehensive information with all the bodies mentioned. And this is in fact what is missing here. And this is not -- it is insufficient and not inaccurate or incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In any event, it is wrong, because where it says president, it should say the Assembly of each of the republics and autonomous provinces. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: It is not incorrect because I must say that this slide or this table is not the only document. You did referred to point 204 where this relation actually is described in these documents and illustrating the relationship between the Assembly, and this as I have said, is insufficient but not incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please let us look at paragraph 197 of your opinion. I quoted it today a little earlier on, and I quote: "That means that four members of the SFRY Presidency could not act on behalf of the SFRY Presidency." And I agree with you on that point. They didn't have a quorum, but they did function nevertheless. And as they functioned, does that mean that they were answerable to their assemblies again, that is, the assemblies of the republics from which they came?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: That's got nothing to do with the responsibility of individual assemblies, and in view of the fact that individual members have not acted correctly as members of the Presidency wanting, for instance, to put forward some stands and also without having the necessary quorum.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But they did operate, and they issued orders to the General Staff. And for those activities, they should have been answerable to the assemblies from which they had come, to which they should have given explanations for their work. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: They have functioned illegally because they did not have any competence to be able to give any such instructions. And within individual assemblies, actually, this should entail some consequences and they should be answerable to their assemblies for such behaviour or acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I agree with you. However, maybe I wouldn't be asking you all these things if you didn't have a footnote here, footnote number 8. And I think you mentioned it today in answer to Mr. Nice's question, and that is that Mr. Slobodan Milosevic refused to take over the powers held by Jovic. But you didn't indicate why he didn't want to do that. He didn't wish to take part in the work of the Presidency because it had decided in favour of the disintegration of Yugoslavia, isn't that so? And then Jovic, several days later, took up his post again.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Well, I believe that this whole question is much more complex than that and calls for taking into consideration a number of elements because of the resignation of President Jovic in itself is something that would call for further explanation and also the interests, for instance, of the defence and the whole defence structure. Then there was also the declarational statement by Milosevic referring to the resignation of Jovic and also reproaching the Presidency from not acting in the interest of Yugoslavia and also demanding from the Serbian Assembly that he be in fact recalled from this function and that another be appointed to this position. And in my view, these acts were not correct, and these elements were also unconstitutional.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I only asked you about something to do with the regulations and how they regulate matters. I don't know if I could be given a few more minutes to deal with the topic related to Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, a few more minutes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 227 it says in your report: "Under the SFRY constitution, the Territorial Defence was an integral part of the armed forces of SFRY. Unlike the JNA, which was a common armed force of the SFRY, the TO was organised at the level of republics and autonomous provinces." This means that there was no single TO in the SFRY but, rather, eight TOs. Therefore, the armed forces of the SFRY were composed of what you say were nine segments, the JNA and eight Territorial Defences; is that right? Professor, isn't that in contradiction with what you said in paragraph 263? The constitution of Yugoslavia followed the concept of common armed forces. Then 264: According to the SFRY constitution, the republics did not have their own armed forces but only the Territorial Defence. The Territorial Defence of the republics and the autonomous provinces together with the JNA constituted the armed forces of the SFRY. So these two are in drastic contradiction, these two positions. Could you explain this to Their Honours?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: This doesn't differ drastically, but the same statement is repeated at another place.
