There is a concept of armed forces of Yugoslavia consisting of two parts of the army and of Territorial Defences which were located at the level of individual republics and provinces because of the interests of the general people's defence. This was the general concept that existed and we have already explained the responsibilities and the relationships of the armies and of the Territorial Defence respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But the concept of all people's defence at the time the constitution was promulgated and you were already a mature and experienced man, I assume you were involved in the drafting of the 1974 constitution. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I don't quite understand your question. The constitution of 1974, as far as the defence is concerned, it was based on the past experience. If you've already asked -- if I dealt with the 1974 constitution, yes. Yes, indeed. I wanted to say how I was involved in the sense of the concept of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to hear whether you were involved in the work on the constitution, but my real question is the following: The principle of all people's defence, did it mean in effect that a situation was created in which each citizen of the SFRY would be armed in the event of the country being in territorial jeopardy should its constitutional order and the boarders of the country be at threat? Wasn't that the idea behind it?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The sense and the concept was to cover the entire territory of the state with the various elements of defence. However, Territorial Defence had to be quickly organised in line with the law -- the law on all people's resistance and other secondary legislation. And outside of this -- these regulations could act on behalf of defence. But they have to be organised within the framework of armed forces. This was already mentioned when we spoke of volunteers and the paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have to be brief. I don't know whether I'll make myself quite clear. I'll do my best. But in paragraph 240, you say that the purpose of Territorial Defence was to organise all people's defence within the framework of the republic and not to activate it in other republics. Should units of the TO from one republic operate in the territory of another republic, they might clash with the TO units of that republic. So could you please explain, if you could, at that point in time, was there any possibility of a collision among the republics in 1974? Was there any real indication that in those years there could be a clash between the republics which would prompt the people to get armed?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Here I think we should understand the context, how the question has been placed. This is a reduction of the -- abbreviation of the text. The question was whether the TO units of Serbia, whether they may operate in another republic in Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and so on. And this was my answer, namely I emphasised the concept of TO, its organisation within the republic, for the defence of the republic and not for operations outside the territory of a given republic. And this was really the point. The TO units are not mobile forces like the JNA. They are territorially organised with elements of responsibility to the bodies of republics, the Presidency of the republic, as well as Presidency of the Federation and the general chiefs of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But a moment ago, you spoke about Article 135 of the SFRY constitution, to the effect that the Republic of Serbia took upon itself all the rights and duties stipulated in the constitution. However, you also added when there was mention in response to Mr. Nice's question that radical changes had taken place only in Serbia, but you might have perhaps told the Judges a little about this declaration on the sovereignty of the Republic of Slovenia, which says in Article 2, the political, economic, and legal system of the Republic of Slovenia is based on the constitution of Slovenia. And then it goes on to say the SFRY constitution, federal laws and other federal enactments are valid in the territory of Slovenia if they are not in contravention of the laws of the Republic of Slovenia. So that is quite opposite to what was stated in the constitution of Serbia of 1990. This declaration says quite the opposite, that the SFRY constitution needed to be in conformity with the constitution of the Republic of Slovenia. Now, how do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Well, in order to answer this question, we'd need more time than we have at our disposal now. I think you should take into account the endeavours of the Republic of Slovenia to ensure a dialogue for the reorganisation of the Federation. Slovenia wasn't satisfied with the request of the position of Serbia. This was reflected in the constitutional debate. And Slovenia issued certain acts and adopted certain acts and discussed this also with other republics. There was also the discussion on confederation. I think that Mr. Milosevic mentioned this. This was on the 28th of September, 1990, and confederation was one of the options of the status.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is my last question. And I should like to draw attention to what is stated in paragraph 245 of your report. The experience of the Republic of Slovenia compared with other republics of the former SFRY where the TO was the most consistently organised demonstrated the advantage of such a concept of organisation. It also proved to be beneficial when the conflict broke out with the JNA after Slovenia declared independence on the 25th of June, 1991. Was the TO of Slovenia at that time already a completely independent armed force or not?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence of Slovenia was equally independent as earlier, but as you know, at the time the relations were acute, and the JNA started with an armed intervention. Units were coming from Croatia, and the Territorial Defence was defending the independence of the Republic of Slovenia. This conflict was resolved rather quickly after the ten year -- ten-day war was ended with the Brioni declaration under the auspices of the European Community. This was recognised, and we accepted a three-month moratorium on the sovereignty and rights of the sovereign republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But that armed force that Slovenia had at its disposal at the time was the Territorial Defence, was it is not? That is my last question.

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Slovenia had at its disposal only the Territorial Defence, because the JNA was acting as a hostile force under quite opposite influences.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A few questions, Professor, which will I hope be susceptible to yes/no answers in light of the time at our disposal. I remind you that the accused asserted to you that there were no armed forces formed by Serbia and that you explained in your evidence-in-chief in relation to volunteers that in exceptional circumstances the President of Serbia might recruit police. It will of course be for the Judges, the Chamber, to decide in due course what type of force constituted armed forces, but help us with this: You said that the president might in certain circumstances recruit police in exceptional circumstances, by which you were describing one of the three particular states, declaration of war and so on. By October 1991, had Serbia ever declared such a state?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: I have no information, no data about that. I tried to explain what the possibilities were for the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I'm --

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: As the police --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. So you have no knowledge of the declaration of such a state. In the absence of such a state, would it have been lawful for the President of Serbia to create police forces?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: My answer would be it would be illegal. So first, this state has to be proclaimed and only then they can be activated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If, contrary to your state of knowledge, a declaration had been made of such a state and if such police forces had been generated, whether police forces in the formal sense or paramilitaries, would the President of Serbia then bear responsibility for their actions?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: Yes, as far as subordination of such police forces to the army, Yugoslav army, of course then that responsibility, accountability, is also at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You answered a question to the effect that Territorial Defence units were essentially restricted to operations within their own republic. Does the same apply for MUP forces, that they are restricted to operation within their own republic?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: All -- there's only the JNA, the volunteers who -- the TO and the volunteers which could be used for the replenishment of the TO ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So the creation of police forces, whether paramilitary or otherwise, and their operating in other states, would that be lawful or unlawful?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: I think that would be outside of the concept of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two questions arising from Articles 83 and 135 of the 1990 Serbian constitution. You've dealt already with how Article 83, subparagraph 5, I think, accords to the president command of the armed forces in peacetime and war. You state that that subarticle or article and its subparagraph does not define armed forces. You allow as your chart shows for the fact that it incorporates the Territorial Defence. Do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: I believe so, yes, because later the Republic of Serbia in its defence law overcame this drawback, and the Article 5 of the defence law defined precisely what the functions of the president of the republic was and how he commands the armed forces concerning organisational matters, personnel matters, also in the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I see we are very nearly at the end of the reasonably allotted time and I have two more questions. Assuming that Article 83, subparagraph 5 by incorporation however imprecisely and unsatisfactorily covers Territorial Defence, does it or not have anything to do with the police or are they to be dealt with separately?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: The police is then dealt with in the defence law in extraordinary special situations. Otherwise, the police units are not used for this purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thus the president's powers in times of peace or war in respect of Territorial Defence is not extended to the police in peacetime, only in wartime or one of the other two states?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: In peacetime, of course police cannot be used for these purposes in peacetime. It is a part of the government and under the competence of the government. So only in these special states of emergency and then they can be activated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Last question relates to the second part of Article 135, and I think we have provided to you and indeed to the Chamber the officially published English version which of course we'll have to have retranslated. But if you'd look, please, in the original at the second part of Article 135 and reflect on how the accused suggested to you that the right for Serbia to act in its own interests under this part of the Article is premised on the disintegration of federal Yugoslavia. Is there anything in that second part that supports that suggestion or is the suggestion that Serbia may act in its own interests when it so judges it more general than that?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: I understood this in the background recrimination of Mr. Milosevic concerning that this has come up in this way, namely that the disintegration was already taking place with Slovenia and Croatia, and as a response to these events --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I understand your narration of what the accused was putting to you, and he said it was a controversial article when drafted and you may know or we may find out by whom it was drafted, but as it reads and interpreting it as a lawyer - we will have a better translation for ourselves later - does it in any way restrict itself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we really must finish. We take no notice of anything that's said before, but allow counsel to ask his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm obliged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does it, as it reads, in any way restrict the liberty of Serbia to act in its own interests to circumstances of the disintegration of the former Yugoslavia or is it more general in its expression?

utterances.speaker: IVAN KRISTAN
utterances.text: It would be difficult for me to assess how -- in general terms, but the second paragraph of Article 135 is considered to be a constitutional basis for the operation of Serbian institutions in Yugoslavia and that -- so that the republic could ensure the compensation for the possible -- the possible losses it would have due to the acts of other republics. I would say that this is setting a constitutional basis for the republican bodies so that nobody would ask them to account for their actions. But the problem here concerning the further process of the crisis of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. We will have a better translation. The article has been referred to by several other witnesses already. I'm grateful for the indulgence of time. I have no further questions of this witness. The Chamber will recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us deal with the witness first of all and finish his evidence. There are -- there are one or two administrative matters I want to deal with. Dr. Kristan, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for allowing me to take the witness stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, are there any matters you want to deal with?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two matters. First of all, to remind the Chamber that in discussing constitutional evidence, the Chamber expressed the view that it would be assisted by a constitutional expert. I think it may have been His Honour Judge Robinson. Therefore, the possibility of our calling a second expert to cover the excluded material relating to Kosovo is before us. You will remember the difficulties we had, as I explained them to you, in identifying suitably qualified witnesses who were able and willing to come. We will renew our efforts to find one of the suitably qualified witnesses, and we will try a get a report on Kosovo which we will serve on you and on the accused and thus on the Court. At the moment I cannot, of course, guarantee that we will either find a witness or if we do there will be time to fit him in, but we will do our best in that regard. There's a matter to be raised in private session with your leave in relation to a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me deal with matter in public session first before we go into private session, and that is to deal with two hearings and the timing of them. Tomorrow's Status Conference on the Defence case I think has been scheduled for 3.00. We will in fact take it at 3.30. If that would be noted. Secondly, concerns Friday the 19th of September and the times of hearing that day. This is due to arrangements which I've made. We will have to finish the sitting that day on the 19th of September at 12.00. So we will sit that day from 9.00 to 12.00. The Prosecution, it means, will be entitled to a further session in their calculation of their times which will be added to the session which was lost, an hour and a half, before the recess. That could be a matter to be dealt with in due course. We will go into private session.
